effect_mechanism: Across sub-practices, agroforestry trees and shrubs add habitat and species diversity relative to the land uses they replace. In India, a Gmelina-mango-pigeon pea system had the largest earthworm Simpson diversity index (0.62) against the smallest in sole pigeon pea (0.41) [ev_biodiversity_outcome_biswas22_1]. A cocoa meta-analysis across ten countries found a significantly higher number of animal species in agroforestry than in monoculture [ev_biodiversity_outcome_niether20_1], and a coffee meta-analysis found bird diversity 120 to 306% higher in three shaded coffee systems than conventional coffee [ev_biodiversity_outcome_jezeer17_2]. In Niger, FMNR adoption increased tree diversity by one to three tree species per farm [ev_biodiversity_outcome_haglund11_1], and a WOCAT compiler for Kenyan FMNR rates both animal diversity and habitat diversity increased, noting many animal species find safe habitats in new FMNR sites [ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_507_2019_animal_diversity, ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_507_2019_habitat_diversity]. In Colombian silvopasture, a global meta-analysis found silvopastoral systems supported 28.4% higher biodiversity than open pastures, with the gain largest for invertebrates (53.7%) [ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_8]; a Colombian World Bank project evaluation reports increased species richness and abundance, including forest-dependent and endangered species [ev_biodiversity_outcome_cmscr20_8], bird monitoring there found four times more birds and 35% higher species richness than grass monocultures, and ant species richness was 62% higher than in treeless pastures [ev_biodiversity_outcome_montagnini15_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_montagnini15_2]. Properties with silvopastoral intervention in the Colombian Amazon significantly reduced deforestation rates compared with control properties [ev_landscape_forest_cover_bur24_2]. For linear plantings, reviews state that windbreaks may help conserve a large number of plant and animal species by providing food, cover from predators, refuge and travel lanes [ev_biodiversity_outcome_harv13_2], that live fences, windbreaks and isolated trees may contribute to biodiversity conservation across fragmented tropical farm landscapes [ev_biodiversity_outcome_harv13_4], and that pastures with isolated trees generally show higher bird diversity than pastures without them [ev_biodiversity_outcome_harv13_1]. A review of silvopastoral research in Central America adds that animals visiting windbreak trees carry and deposit tree seeds, letting woody species persist and potentially re-establish in the pasture landscape, and cites a Costa Rican study finding significantly greater seed-rain density and species richness in windbreaks than in open pasture [ev_biodiversity_outcome_dagang03_4]. Farmers in Colombia and Costa Rica report that live fences increase landscape connectivity, creating local corridors for fauna and flora, which they see as positive for native biodiversity [ev_biodiversity_outcome_moran18_6]. A tropical agroforestry meta-analysis found natural enemies of pests significantly more abundant under agroforestry than in controls [ev_biodiversity_outcome_pumarino15_1]. A global silvopastoral meta-analysis breaks the 28.4% biodiversity gain down further: native-tree silvopasture held 36.3% more biodiversity than open pasture and planted-tree silvopasture held 20.9% more, with invertebrate abundance specifically about 60% higher under native-tree silvopasture [ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_2, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_3, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_10, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_12]. A further Colombian Andes study of dung beetles — an indicator of ecological-process recovery, not just species counts — found significantly more beetles caught per trap in intensive silvopasture than in the treeless improved pasture it replaced (275 individuals across five species against 143 across three species), with the same three species found in both land uses plus two additional species recorded only in the silvopastoral system [ev_biodiversity_outcome_giraldo10_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_giraldo10_2].
conditionality: The roll-up reads strong because its strongest-evidenced sub-practices do: silvopastoral, shaded perennial-crop and planted silvoarable systems each read a strong gain on their own, and none of the remaining sub-practices (cross-family, linear-boundary, regeneration-based farmland, each reading only a slight gain) is large or negative enough to pull the pooled picture down or flip the direction. Set against the gains, when traditional shaded coffee/cacao agroforest is intensified to sparse-shade plantation, a global meta-analysis found total species richness fell 46% and forest-species richness fell 65%, and converting natural forest to agroforest itself cost 11% of total species richness and 35% of forest-species richness — measured harm from two independent sources, read against intensification and against standing forest rather than against open farmland [ev_biodiversity_outcome_debeen13_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_debeen13_2, ev_biodiversity_outcome_debeen13_3, ev_biodiversity_outcome_debeen13_4]. In Cameroon, cocoa yields above 1 t/ha were not attainable with more than 10 associated tree species, a direct yield-biodiversity trade-off [ev_biodiversity_outcome_seghieri19_7]. effect_mechanism: On pastoral rangeland, trees raise biodiversity mainly by adding habitat structure and by supporting seed dispersal into the pasture. A global meta-analysis of silvopastoral systems (47 publications, 279 comparisons) found biodiversity 28.4% higher in silvopasture than in open pastures; broken down by system type, silvopasture built around existing native trees held 36.3% more biodiversity than open pasture and silvopasture with planted trees held 20.9% more, with invertebrate biodiversity specifically 53.7% higher under native-tree silvopasture [ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_12, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_2, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_3, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_8]. In Costa Rican cattle pastures, a review of Central American silvopastoral research reports that windbreak trees support seed rain — animals visiting the trees carry and deposit tree seeds, letting woody species persist and potentially re-establish in the landscape — and cites a study finding significantly greater seed-rain density and species richness in windbreaks than in open pasture [ev_biodiversity_outcome_dagang03_4].
conditionality: A related measure from the same global meta-analysis — invertebrate abundance, as distinct from the invertebrate biodiversity/richness figure above — found a large point estimate under native-tree silvopasture (+60%) that was not statistically significant [ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_10], which is part of why agreement, not strength, holds the class at moderate rather than strong. The meta-analysis is a global pooled result with no country or income-group breakdown of its own, so only the Costa Rican windbreak-seed-rain finding ties this row to a named country; Costa Rica is high income, so while the global meta-analysis evidence transfers only loosely to the LIC/LMIC target, the row as a whole transfers as adjacent rather than squarely in context [ev_biodiversity_outcome_dagang03_4].

effect_mechanism: Across sub-practices pooled together, agroforestry trees and shrubs are reported to add habitat and pest-control value. A tropical-agroforestry review states that live fences, windbreaks and isolated trees may contribute to biodiversity conservation, and that retaining or establishing trees in agricultural land may be a critical component of conservation efforts in fragmented landscapes, with floristic diversity that can be high and a substantial number of animal species able to exploit these habitats for feeding, movement and, in some cases, reproduction [ev_biodiversity_outcome_harv13_4]. A meta-analysis of tropical agroforestry studies found natural enemies of pests were significantly more abundant under agroforestry than in controls, as part of a general benefit to natural pest control [ev_biodiversity_outcome_pumarino15_1]. A separate perspective review states that agroforestry is likely to have biodiversity benefits compared to conventional arable, pasture or forestry, though this depends on the variety, abundance and ecological suitability of the tree species used [ev_biodiversity_outcome_seddon21_3].
conditionality: The same meta-analysis that found more natural enemies also reports, for the diversity (rather than abundance) of natural enemies, that most studies (7 of 11) showed no effect and the response of predation and parasitism was mixed, with 3 of the 7 studies showing no effect and the rest split evenly between positive and negative — held out here as a finding on a narrower measure of the same taxon group, not a contradiction of the abundance result [ev_biodiversity_outcome_pumarino15_2]. The review-level units generalise across cited studies rather than measuring anything themselves, and the review qualifies that agroforestry elements 'are not substitutes for the original vegetation' and that almost all its cited studies were in landscapes with some remnant forest nearby, so element value and landscape context are confounded [ev_biodiversity_outcome_harv13_4]. None of the four units names a country, income group or farming system for this pooled row, so although the pattern is consistent it only transfers as adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target [ev_biodiversity_outcome_harv13_4, ev_biodiversity_outcome_pumarino15_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_pumarino15_2, ev_biodiversity_outcome_seddon21_3].

effect_mechanism: Linear plantings add woody habitat structure to farmland. A tropical-agroforestry review states that, depending on their floristic diversity, structural complexity and management, windbreaks may help conserve a large number of plant and animal species, including a limited number of forest-dependent species, by providing food, cover from predators, refuge and travel lanes [ev_biodiversity_outcome_harv13_2]. A review of silvopastoral research in Central America adds that animals visiting windbreak trees carry and deposit tree seeds, letting woody species persist and potentially re-establish in the pasture landscape, and cites a Costa Rican study finding significantly greater seed-rain density and species richness in windbreaks than in open pasture [ev_biodiversity_outcome_dagang03_4]. In Colombia and Costa Rica, farmers report that planting live fences increases landscape connectivity, creating local corridors that both fauna and flora can use, which they see as positive for native biodiversity conservation [ev_biodiversity_outcome_moran18_6]. The same review also reports a mixed case: in Queensland, Australia, planted eucalyptus windbreaks were useful habitat for some bird species but insignificant habitat for mammals and rainforest specialists, and held much lower value as wildlife habitat than riparian vegetation, which the authors attribute to the windbreaks' lower structural complexity and single-species planting [ev_biodiversity_outcome_harv13_3].
conditionality: The class stays slight because one of the three units finds no added value for mammals and forest specialists relative to riparian habitat, holding agreement at medium rather than high [ev_biodiversity_outcome_harv13_3]. None of the three states a size for the conservation gain: the windbreak review is a generalisation across cited temperate studies, the live-fence unit is a farmer-perception survey across Colombia and Costa Rica (upper-middle and high income), and neither names the countries, income group or farming system behind the pooled row, which is why confidence stays low and the row only transfers as adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target [ev_biodiversity_outcome_harv13_2, ev_biodiversity_outcome_moran18_6, ev_biodiversity_outcome_harv13_3].

effect_mechanism: On red and lateritic soils in Jhargram, West Bengal, India, an agri-horti-silviculture system of Gmelina arborea and grafted mango trees with pigeon pea grown in the alleys had the highest earthworm diversity of the systems compared, with a Simpson's diversity index of 0.62 against 0.41 in sole pigeon pea [ev_biodiversity_outcome_biswas22_1]. Tree prunings and leaf fall were kept in the field.
conditionality: The strong class rests on a single trial and a single taxon: earthworm diversity is a soil-biodiversity indicator, not a measure of wider farm or landscape biodiversity, and statistical significance of the difference is not reported [ev_biodiversity_outcome_biswas22_1]. The system was fertilised and given need-based irrigation at tree establishment, so the result applies to managed alley systems on degraded lateritic soils in lower-middle-income settings; further studies, on other taxa, are needed before this reads as a general effect.

The Niger result is a matched comparison of adopters with non-adopters that counts tree species on farms, not wider biodiversity [ev_biodiversity_outcome_haglund11_1]. The evidence comes from a narrow base in Kenya and Niger, so confidence is medium.

effect_mechanism: In shaded coffee and cacao systems, more structurally complex agroforestry supports more species than simpler, intensified alternatives. A ten-country cocoa meta-analysis found cocoa agroforestry held a significantly higher number of animal species, pooled across taxa, than cocoa monoculture [ev_biodiversity_outcome_niether20_1]. A review of shaded coffee systems found bird diversity 120 to 306% higher in three shaded coffee systems of varying complexity than in conventional coffee [ev_biodiversity_outcome_jezeer17_2]. Comparing coffee/cacao agroforest against a more intensified sparse-shade plantation, a response-ratio study found total species richness and forest-species richness both significantly higher under agroforest [ev_biodiversity_outcome_debeen13_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_debeen13_2]. Along a Mexican coffee-intensification gradient (forest, traditional polyculture, commercial polyculture, shaded monoculture), estimated ant, butterfly and bird richness was higher at the less-intensified, more complex-shade end of the gradient that agroforestry occupies [ev_biodiversity_outcome_perf05_1].
conditionality: Set against the gains, the same response-ratio study found coffee/cacao agroforest itself held significantly lower richness than standing natural forest — 11% lower for total species richness and 35% lower for forest-species richness — so the biodiversity benefit is relative to a more intensified system, not to the forest it may have replaced [ev_biodiversity_outcome_debeen13_3, ev_biodiversity_outcome_debeen13_4]. In Cameroon, cocoa yields above 1 t/ha were not attainable with more than 10 associated tree species, a direct trade-off between tree diversity and cocoa yield that growers face as they add species [ev_biodiversity_outcome_seghieri19_7]. Most units describe a significant difference without naming every taxon or giving a consistent metric across studies, and the certification, intensification-gradient and cocoa meta-analysis evidence does not enumerate study countries in the cited text, so the row sits in_context with, but is not a close match for, the LIC/LMIC target as a whole [ev_biodiversity_outcome_niether20_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_debeen13_1].

effect_mechanism: In Colombian silvopastoral systems, biodiversity rises relative to open pasture, the land use the practice replaces. A global meta-analysis (47 publications, 279 comparisons) found silvopastoral systems supported 28.4% higher biodiversity than open pastures, with native-tree silvopasture raising biodiversity by 36.3% and planted-tree silvopasture by 20.9%, both against open pastures [ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_2, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_3, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_12]. Invertebrate abundance showed the largest taxon-specific gain against open pasture, 53.7% [ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_8]. In Colombia specifically, a World Bank project evaluation reports that silvopastoral systems played a major role in increasing and conserving biodiversity at farm and landscape level, raising the number of species (richness) and individuals observed (abundance), including forest-dependent and endangered species [ev_biodiversity_outcome_cmscr20_8]; bird monitoring on Colombian cattle farms found intensive silvopasture had four times more birds and 35% higher species richness than grass monocultures, and ant species richness was 62% higher than in treeless pastures in the same landscape [ev_biodiversity_outcome_montagnini15_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_montagnini15_2]. Properties with silvopastoral intervention in the Colombian Amazon also significantly reduced deforestation rates compared with control properties [ev_landscape_forest_cover_bur24_2]. A tropical-agroforestry review states that pastures with isolated trees generally show higher bird diversity than pastures without them [ev_biodiversity_outcome_harv13_1]. A further Colombian Andes study of dung beetles — an indicator of ecological-process recovery, not just species counts — found significantly more beetles caught per trap in intensive silvopasture than in the treeless improved pasture it replaced (275 individuals across five species against 143 across three species), with the same three species found in both land uses plus two additional species recorded only in the silvopastoral system [ev_biodiversity_outcome_giraldo10_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_giraldo10_2].
conditionality: The same global meta-analysis measures silvopasture against a second, different benchmark — ungrazed native forest — and there the sign reverses: native-tree silvopasture held 18.1% lower overall biodiversity, 14.8% lower plant biodiversity and 24.4% lower invertebrate biodiversity than native forest, with invertebrate abundance 30.2% lower [ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_4, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_5, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_9, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_11]. This is a conservation benchmark, not the intervention counterfactual: it means silvopasture holds less biodiversity than intact forest, not that converting grazing land to silvopasture reduces biodiversity, so the class is set from the open-pasture comparisons and these forest-benchmark units are held out of it. Two further forest-benchmark comparisons, for birds and bird species richness, found no significant difference, and the invertebrate-abundance gain against open pasture was itself not significant despite a large point estimate [ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_6, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_7, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_10]. The meta-analysis does not report the countries behind its figures, so only the Colombian project evidence anchors this row to the LIC/LMIC target; as a pooled global figure it transfers only as adjacent [ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_cmscr20_8]. The bird-diversity review's single worked example compares recently abandoned pasture against actively grazed pasture, so grazing cessation is confounded with the trees themselves [ev_biodiversity_outcome_harv13_1]. These two new dung-beetle units read as a benefit and are weighted heavily enough, alongside the existing Colombian evidence, to move this row's own class from a moderate to a strong gain; they do not touch the separate forest-benchmark comparisons already held out of the class above.

effect_mechanism: The carbon evidence splits by sub-practice. Silvopastoral systems read strongest on their own, planted silvoarable and regeneration-based farmland read a moderate gain, and cross-family and linear-boundary readings are only slight — so the roll-up states a moderate gain rather than the pooled slight reading. In Colombia, a World Bank project evaluation reports net accumulated CO2 removals of 1,131,056 t CO2e from converting pasturelands to dispersed trees, live fences and intensive silvopastoral systems [ev_carbon_sequestration_cmscr20_10], Costa Rican silvopastoral systems had a carbon storage potential of 1.2 to 4.5 Mg C/ha/yr against below 1 Mg C/ha/yr in treeless pasture [ev_carbon_sequestration_montagnini15_1], and a global land-use-conversion meta-analysis found soil organic carbon rose 31 to 66% converting agriculture to silvopasture [ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_27, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_39]. In Ethiopia, FMNR-based reforestation projects audited by forestry experts sequestered 181,650 and 94,817 tonnes of CO2 at two sites since 2007 [ev_carbon_sequestration_wvfmnr19_11]. Under regeneration-based parkland systems, soil carbon is reported 46% higher under Faidherbia albida canopy than outside it in Senegal [ev_soil_organic_carbon_faosen24_1], a pan-Sahelian review of shrub and tree parklands found soil total carbon 20 to 75% higher under woody canopies than open fields [ev_soil_organic_carbon_felix18_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_felix18_2], and in Honduras, organic matter content in Quesungual fields rose from 2.4% to 4.5% over four years [ev_soil_organic_carbon_welc02_3]. A WOCAT compiler for Kenyan FMNR rates carbon and greenhouse-gas sequestration strongly increased, citing tree-cover gain through afforestation or FMNR as a way to sequester carbon in biomass [ev_carbon_sequestration_wocat_507_2019_emission_of_carbon_and_greenhouse_gases]. For linear and cross-family plantings, a review of East African agroforestry found aboveground carbon of 26.7 Mg C/ha held in trees on boundaries [ev_carbon_sequestration_muthuri23_5], and a pan-tropical soil study found agroforestry significantly raised soil organic carbon by an overall effect size of 1.21 compared with crop monocultures, with a 40% rise in soil organic carbon, 13% in nitrogen storage and 50% lower soil erosion [ev_soil_organic_carbon_muchane20_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_muchane20_2]. The IPCC AR6 AFOLU chapter cites a global technical mitigation potential of 9.4 GtCO2eq/yr for agroforestry [ev_carbon_sequestration_ipccar6_3]. In the Colombian Amazon (Caquetá), a chronosequence study of silvopastoral systems converted from Brachiaria pasture found no significant change in total soil organic carbon stock over the full sampled soil profile against the traditional pasture it replaced, but did find a soil-carbon gain in the deepest sampled layer, which the authors read as showing the practice could turn the soil into a carbon sink in deeper layers over time [ev_soil_organic_carbon_olaya20_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_olaya20_2]. A review of pastures in semi-arid north-eastern Brazil also reports that retaining native trees (Ziziphus joazeiro and Spondias tuberosa) in pasture significantly raised total soil carbon compared with open pasture away from the trees, though it gives no carbon value [ev_soil_organic_carbon_dagang03_1]. In Ghana, a plot-survey model of hybrid cocoa found that moderate shade gave a net greenhouse-gas removal increment of 127%, or 3.7 Mg CO2eq per hectare per year, over full or near-full sun hybrid cocoa [ev_carbon_sequestration_hawkins24_1]. In Nicaragua, traditional diverse-shade coffee held more above-ground tree carbon than simplified commercial shade coffee -- 41 against 16 t C/ha, measured from one sampled plot per farm (10 traditional-polyculture farms, 11 commercial-polyculture farms) [ev_carbon_sequestration_rahn14_1]. A biodrainage strip planting of Eucalyptus tereticornis along waterlogged, canal-irrigated fields in northwest India sequestered a total of 15.5 t C/ha in timber, fuelwood, twigs/leaves and roots by the time the trees (240 surviving per ha) were harvested at just over five years old [ev_carbon_sequestration_ram11_7].
conditionality: Almost none of this evidence is a measured net CO2e balance for the practice itself: most of it is modelled regional or global mitigation potential (IPCC, Roe et al.), a carbon stock without a time denominator, or a single-gas figure, which is why confidence stays only medium despite the growing pool of 100 units and high agreement on direction. Held against the pattern, in Niger after four years scattered Ziziphus trees raised soil carbon by 5 to 10% and nitrogen by 10 to 15%, but the differences were not significant [ev_soil_organic_carbon_bado21_1], and in Ethiopia soil organic carbon, total nitrogen and other chemical and physical soil properties did not significantly differ under versus outside Faidherbia albida canopy at the end of one season [ev_soil_organic_carbon_sida18_1]. Converting existing forest to agroforestry is also measured as a loss in several readings of the same global meta-analysis — not the adoption pathway this cell is about — and the silvopastoral gains sit mostly in upper-middle-income Colombia and high-income Costa Rica, so the row transfers only as adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target despite the strong Latin American silvopastoral signal [ev_carbon_sequestration_montagnini15_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_cmscr20_10]. The Colombian Amazon system was established on tilled, limed, phosphate-treated and re-seeded pasture alongside the new trees, so the deeper-layer gain cannot be credited to the trees alone, and the full-profile result found no significant change at all, adding a null to the pool rather than strengthening the gain. This Ghanaian estimate is modelled rather than directly measured and compares two shade densities within the same cocoa system rather than agroforestry against no trees at all; the authors note the shade contrast is confounded by differences in fertiliser use and hand pollination between the plots surveyed, so it adds a lower-middle-income data point without moving the row off its existing moderate reading [ev_carbon_sequestration_hawkins24_1]. The Brazilian pasture soil-carbon finding is likewise a narrative review of an underlying primary study rather than a new measurement, and adds further upper-middle-income Brazilian evidence to the row's existing adjacent transfer [ev_soil_organic_carbon_dagang03_1]. This Nicaraguan comparison is a carbon stock, not a sequestration rate, and the reported ranges (8 to 104 against 4 to 39 t C/ha) overlap widely with no significance test reported [ev_carbon_sequestration_rahn14_1]. That Indian figure is a one-off harvest measurement from a single planting, occupying only the strips themselves within the field rather than the whole farmed area, and is a stock at harvest, not an annual sequestration rate [ev_carbon_sequestration_ram11_7].

A review of Colombian intensive silvopastoral systems reports a preliminary greenhouse-gas balance in which lower nitrogen losses and higher carbon capture offset the systems' methane emissions from livestock [ev_carbon_sequestration_murg13_2]. effect_mechanism: In tree-perennial systems (shaded coffee, cocoa and similar tree crops), carbon accumulates mainly in the aboveground biomass of the shade trees and the crop together, with soil carbon showing a more mixed picture. A pan-tropical review of cocoa agroforestry (across Ghana, Bolivia, Indonesia and other countries) found total biomass carbon (above- and below-ground, cocoa plus shade trees) on average 2.5 times higher than in cocoa monoculture [ev_carbon_sequestration_niether20_1]. In Ghana, a model of currently recommended shade-tree densities in Hybrid cocoa found a net greenhouse-gas removal increment of 127% (3.7 Mg CO2 equivalent per ha per year) over the unshaded baseline [ev_carbon_sequestration_hawkins24_1]. In Costa Rica, an eight-year eddy-covariance measurement of coffee agroforestry plots (trees, coffee, litter and soil together) found mean carbon storage of 3.6 tonnes of carbon per ha per year [ev_carbon_sequestration_seghieri19_5], and a review reports 29.8 Mg of carbon per ha more in the aboveground biomass of shaded coffee plots than in full-sun coffee plantations [ev_carbon_sequestration_villa20_6]. A systematic review of East African agroforestry found aboveground carbon in perennial tree-crop systems averaging 29.9 ± 12.7 Mg of carbon per ha [ev_carbon_sequestration_muthuri23_4], and the same review's modelled estimates for Ethiopian enset-coffee and tree-coffee systems translate to biomass carbon of 139.5 and 153.4 Mg per ha respectively, against 96.6 Mg per ha for enset-tree alone [ev_carbon_sequestration_muthuri23_6]. A global review of coffee agroforestry reports soil organic matter improved by 20 to 35% under shade [ev_soil_organic_carbon_patil25_5]. In Nicaragua, traditional diverse-shade coffee held more above-ground tree carbon than simplified commercial shade coffee -- 41 against 16 t C/ha, measured from one sampled plot per farm (10 traditional-polyculture farms, 11 commercial-polyculture farms) [ev_carbon_sequestration_rahn14_1].
conditionality: The soil-carbon signal is not uniform: the same pan-tropical cocoa review that found the large biomass-carbon gain found no significant difference in soil organic carbon or total soil carbon between cocoa agroforestry and monoculture, the one exception among soil chemical properties being higher soil pH in monoculture [ev_soil_organic_carbon_niether20_1] — so the strong class rests on aboveground biomass carbon, not soil carbon. The Ethiopian enset-coffee and tree-coffee figures are modelled with the CO2FIX model and exceed the review's own regional empirical estimates, and are specific to those crops rather than the practice generally [ev_carbon_sequestration_muthuri23_6]. The Costa Rican eddy-covariance figure is also a measured storage figure before deducting carbon exported from the system in harvested coffee and pruned wood over the same period [ev_carbon_sequestration_seghieri19_5]. The evidence spans lower-middle-income West Africa and East Africa, high-income Costa Rica, and upper-middle-income Latin American and Southeast Asian cocoa countries, so while most units sit inside the LIC/LMIC target, the class draws on some high-income evidence too. This Nicaraguan comparison is a carbon stock, not a sequestration rate, and the reported ranges (8 to 104 against 4 to 39 t C/ha) overlap widely with no significance test reported [ev_carbon_sequestration_rahn14_1].

effect_mechanism: Pooled across sub-practices, modelled mitigation-potential and stock-comparison studies consistently find a carbon benefit, though almost none of them gives a measured net CO2e balance for the practice. A pan-tropical soil study (71 studies, 225 pairs) found agroforestry significantly increased soil organic carbon storage compared with crop monocultures (overall effect size 1.21) and reduced soil erosion by 50%, with soil organic carbon up 40%, nitrogen storage up 13%, available nitrogen up 46% and available phosphorus up 11% [ev_soil_organic_carbon_muchane20_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_muchane20_2]. The IPCC AR6 AFOLU chapter cites a global analysis estimating agroforestry's technical mitigation potential at 9.4 GtCO2eq/yr, and further estimates a technical potential of 4.1 (0.3–9.4) GtCO2eq/yr for 2020-2050, of which 0.8 (0.4–1.1) GtCO2eq/yr is available at USD100/tCO2 [ev_carbon_sequestration_ipccar6_3, ev_carbon_sequestration_ipccar6_5]. A regional modelling study finds agroforestry's mitigation density about 45 tCO2eq/ha, and across the Africa-Middle East region its cost-effective mitigation potential at 0.19 GtCO2eq/yr (8% of the regional total) [ev_carbon_sequestration_roe21_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_roe21_2]. In Brazil, a review reports agroforestry carbon sequestration rates varying by climate from 954 to 3670 tCO2/km2/yr, with a technical potential of 0.1 to 5.7 GtCO2eq/yr, the largest among the land uses it compared [ev_carbon_sequestration_santos25_3]. One directly measured finding in the row combines biomass and soil carbon sequestration with changes in net CH4 and N2O emissions and estimates a shift to agroforestry can mitigate 27.2 t CO2eq/ha/yr, at least over the early growth stage up to an average age of 14 years [ev_carbon_sequestration_kim16_1]. The Regreening Africa endline survey found a relative 3% increase in soil organic carbon compared with baseline, with significant variation across countries and sites [ev_soil_organic_carbon_rgaf23_2].
conditionality: Only one of these 67 units — the biomass-plus-soil-plus-gas estimate above — is a measured net balance for the practice itself; the rest are modelled regional or global mitigation potentials, single-gas or stock-only figures, or review restatements of other studies, so the engine cannot let most of them set the class, which is why confidence stays very low despite the consistent direction. A further eight units are held out because their comparator is existing natural forest, not the farming system the practice would actually replace: converting forest to agroforestry lost soil organic carbon in every reading — 22 to 26% at shallow depth and 24% for agrisilviculture specifically — and forest-to-silvopastoral/agrosilvopastoral conversions likewise lost 27 to 36% at various depths, reversals that describe deforestation for agroforestry, not the cropland- or pasture-to-agroforestry adoption pathway this cell is about [ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_2, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_10, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_14, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_25, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_37]. effect_mechanism: Trees planted into cropland add carbon to the soil through leaf litter, prunings and roots, raising soil carbon storage above that of the crop grown alone. In a ten-year trial on degraded red and lateritic soil in West Bengal, India, soil organic carbon under a Gmelina-mango-pigeon pea alley system reached 0.59% against 0.34% under sole pigeon pea, from an initial 0.30% [ev_soil_organic_carbon_biswas22_1]. A global meta-analysis found that converting cropland to agroforestry generally increased soil carbon storage, consistent with earlier syntheses [ev_soil_organic_carbon_ma20_3]. In southern Malawi, Tephrosia vogelii relay-planted under maize keeps growing into the dry season and returns nitrogen-rich leafy residues; at Songani soil C under this intercrop was 1.57 against 1.46 under monoculture maize [ev_soil_organic_carbon_snapp10_1]. A biodrainage strip planting of Eucalyptus tereticornis along waterlogged, canal-irrigated fields in northwest India sequestered a total of 15.5 t C/ha in timber, fuelwood, twigs/leaves and roots by the time the trees (240 surviving per ha) were harvested at just over five years old [ev_carbon_sequestration_ram11_7].
conditionality: The direction is consistent, but not every site shows a clear gain. The Malawi difference was a trend that was not significant (P value = 0.10) [ev_soil_organic_carbon_snapp10_1], and at Sadore, Niger, the block with Ziziphus mauritiana trees held from 5 to 10 % more soil organic carbon than the block without after four years of millet and cowpea, a difference that was not significant [ev_soil_organic_carbon_bado21_1]. The Niger trial compares two blocks with tree presence neither randomised nor replicated, so block differences are mixed into the contrast [ev_soil_organic_carbon_bado21_1]. Soil carbon is a component of carbon removal, measured here as a stock or concentration, not as a removal rate, and tree biomass storage is not counted in this row [ev_soil_organic_carbon_biswas22_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_snapp10_1]. The strongest gain comes from a long-running research-station trial on degraded soil, where the starting carbon was low [ev_soil_organic_carbon_biswas22_1]. The field evidence is from low-income Malawi and Niger and lower-middle-income India, all rainfed cropping; the meta-analysis is global [ev_soil_organic_carbon_snapp10_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_bado21_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_biswas22_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_ma20_3]. effect_mechanism: In Colombia and Costa Rica, silvopastoral systems are reported to raise carbon stocks and sequestration. The World Bank's Colombian Conservation and Sustainable Development of the Coffee Growing Regions project reports net accumulated CO2 removals of 1,131,056 t CO2e from converting pasturelands to dispersed trees in pasture, live fences, intensive silvopastoral systems and secondary-forest conservation [ev_carbon_sequestration_cmscr20_10]. In Costa Rica, silvopastoral systems had a carbon storage potential of 1.2 to 4.5 Mg C/ha/yr, against below 1 Mg C/ha/yr in treeless pasture [ev_carbon_sequestration_montagnini15_1]. A global meta-analysis of land-use conversions found soil organic carbon stocks rose 66% and 31% at different depths converting agriculture to silvopasture, 17% converting forest plantation to silvopasture, and 32% converting forest to silvopasture at the deepest sampled profile, where the authors note silvopasture held more SOC than the forest it replaced at that depth [ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_27, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_39, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_24, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_38]. A Colombian review states a preliminary GHG balance where lower nitrogen losses and greater carbon capture in intensive silvopastoral systems offset livestock methane emissions [ev_carbon_sequestration_murg13_2], and silvopastoral systems built from degraded natural woodland are reported to mitigate climate change by increasing above- and below-ground carbon stocks [ev_carbon_sequestration_taboada20_4]. Among pasture-improvement practices assessed in a Colombian climate-smart-agriculture matrix, only tree-improved pastures and live fences showed a positive effect on the mitigation pillar [ev_carbon_sequestration_taboada20_6]. Properties with silvopastoral intervention in the Colombian Amazon also significantly reduced deforestation rates compared with control properties, retaining forest carbon [ev_landscape_forest_cover_bur24_2]. In the Colombian Amazon (Caquetá), a chronosequence comparing silvopasture against the traditional pasture it replaced found no significant change in total soil organic carbon stock over the full sampled soil profile, but did find a gain confined to the deepest sampled layer, read by the authors as a sign the practice could turn the soil into a carbon sink in deeper layers over time [ev_soil_organic_carbon_olaya20_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_olaya20_2]. A review of pastures in semi-arid north-eastern Brazil reports a similar pattern: retaining native tree species (Ziziphus joazeiro and Spondias tuberosa) in pasture significantly raised total soil carbon compared with open pasture away from the trees, attributed to litterfall and fine-root turnover adding soil organic matter and to nitrogen fixation, though the review gives no carbon value [ev_soil_organic_carbon_dagang03_1].

conditionality: Both readings come from one silvopasture experiment in the Canterbury Plains of New Zealand, high-income temperate evidence well outside the LIC/LMIC target, so the row transfers as out of context. effect_mechanism: Trees on farms slightly reduce the damage drought does to farm households. In Isiolo County communities in Kenya, households rated agroforestry important during drought, a farmer said deep-rooted mango trees get water from deep down, others said trees do not dry up fast and keep producing fruit when there is no rain, and 74% of respondents had planted trees with drought in mind; the study concludes that agroforestry can and does build livelihood resilience to drought [ev_t3_drought_importance_quandt17_8, ev_t3_drought_deeproots_quandt17_7, ev_t3_drought_farmerquote_quandt17_12, ev_t3_drought_intentional_quandt17_14, ev_t3_drought_conclusion_quandt17_10]. Reviews report that under drought understorey crop yields could be higher than in an open system even in intense shade, and that live fences supply livestock fodder when pasture is scarce [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13, ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1]. In an eastern Canadian soybean intercrop, experimentally induced drought caused crop losses in the monocrop only (Nasielski et al. 2015) [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4]. The Kenyan FMNR WOCAT sheet rates drought impacts as reduced, its compiler judging that FMNR improves micro-climate and soil moisture and therefore mitigates the impact of droughts [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. In Lempira, Honduras, a practitioner article on the Quesungual slash-and-mulch system reports that, compared with farmers who remained with slash-and-burn, Quesungual farmers did not experience a total loss in maize production during the dry period of El Niño in 1997, which the authors put down to improved soil conditions [ev_drought_hazard_welc02_2]. In a French walnut-based alley-cropping system, an imposed spring drought cut full-sun pea yield by 22% while the alley-cropped yield was relatively improved by 12 to 20% against its own rainfed baseline [ev_drought_hazard_blan22_3].
conditionality: Effects are not uniform, and for some adopters the trees made drought losses worse. A multi-species silvopasture trial on degraded rangeland in arid India found the same kind of reversal in a grazing system: understorey herbage yield fell further under drought beneath every tree and shrub species than in the treeless control pasture, attributed by the authors to shading and competition for soil moisture; the trees did supply extra dry-season browse fodder, a trade-off kept separate from the herbage finding [ev_drought_hazard_singhrao08_1]. effect_mechanism: IPCC assessments link agroforestry to food security through diversification of production that avoids trade-offs between crop and tree products, and an East African systematic review finds that the fodder, food, firewood and income from agroforestry act as safety nets in climate shocks [ev_food_security_ipccar6ch5_7, ev_food_security_muthuri23_1]. The IPCC land report estimates that up to 1.3 billion people on degrading land could benefit in food security through agroforestry [ev_food_security_ipccsrccl6_6]. Under Regreening Africa the share of respondents consuming at least five of the ten food items rose from 16 to 21, a 31 percent increase, and households that intensified their use of tree products saw significant gains in dietary diversity [ev_food_security_rgaf23_8, ev_food_security_rgaf23_10]. In the Nepal mid-hills the share of food-sufficient households rose from 52% to 69% after a market-oriented agroforestry project [ev_food_security_pandit19_1]. In Nyando, Kenya, agroforestry-project households used fewer detrimental coping strategies in hunger periods and some relied on tree fruit when floods washed crops away, and in Rwanda tree density was associated with higher food security in some agroecologies [ev_food_security_thorlak12_2, ev_food_security_thorlak12_1, ev_food_security_ndoli21_1]. A global review of nature-based solutions for food security cites population-survey studies finding better food access where agroforestry was applied in southern Africa, Brazil and China over periods of up to 20 years [ev_food_security_nguy24n_1]. A systematic review of agroforestry adoption in sub-Saharan Africa, mostly from Ethiopia, Kenya and Malawi, finds that agroforestry recurrently enhances dietary diversity, particularly where fruit- and vegetable-producing trees are included [ev_food_security_jemaneh26_1]. In the East Usambara Mountains, Tanzania, improved agroforestry secured enough food throughout the year for 40% of households against 18% of households using traditional practices [ev_food_security_reyes05_1].
conditionality: Few units say how big the effect is, so the class is capped at moderate. In Rwanda's Buberuka Highlands more trees went with lower food security, a measured harm, while in Congo Nile the association ran the other way [ev_food_security_ndoli21_2]. The Regreening Africa FIES score showed no substantial change, moving from 4.9 to 4.8, and the Campbell systematic review found the impact on nutrition and food security beneficial or neutral across the studies it covered [ev_food_security_rgaf23_9, ev_food_security_castle21s_4]. The Regreening Africa and Nepal results are before-and-after surveys with no control group, and the Nepal project bundled the trees with market linkage, training, subsidies and organic fertiliser [ev_food_security_rgaf23_8, ev_food_security_pandit19_1]. The Tanzanian comparison is a household survey without randomisation: the improved farms bundled trees with cash crops, manure and dairy cattle, were larger and had more off-farm income, so part of the food-sufficiency gap is a livestock and wealth effect [ev_food_security_reyes05_1]. The sub-Saharan review notes that outcomes vary with agroforestry type, complementary practices and the wider context, and gives no pooled food-security estimate [ev_food_security_jemaneh26_1]. The IPCC figure is a count of people who could benefit, not a measured effect [ev_food_security_ipccsrccl6_6]. The food-access review included only studies showing improvement in at least one food-security dimension, so its finding says nothing about studies that found no benefit, and one of its cited studies is a life-cycle assessment rather than a population survey [ev_food_security_nguy24n_1]. effect_mechanism: Trees cool the air and soil that crops and livestock experience, through shade and altered radiation and humidity. In Ethiopia, air temperature at wheat floral height was lowered by up to 6°C at midday under Faidherbia albida canopy compared with the open field, reaching a maximum of 29°C under the canopy against 36°C in the open, and temperature stayed above 28°C for about six hours a day in the open field against under two hours under the canopy [ev_microclimate_buffering_sida18_1]. In Germany, poplar alley cropping measured 3.4°C lower air temperature than sole wheat on hot summer days [ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_4]. A meta-analysis of Chinese farmland shelterbelts found summer air temperature significantly reduced by 4.01% compared with unsheltered farmland [ev_microclimate_buffering_hao26_1]. In Sahelian parklands, trees reduce the maximum daily temperature by an average of 1 to 2.5°C, with stronger effects on hotter, drier days, and under Acacia tortilis canopy in Senegal's Ferlo, air temperatures ranged from 29 to 36°C against 26 to 42°C outside the canopy [ev_microclimate_buffering_bayala14_2, ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_6]. In cocoa agroforestry across ten countries, the canopy of shade trees keeps mean temperature lower and buffers daily maximum and minimum temperatures compared with monoculture [ev_microclimate_buffering_niether20_1]. For livestock, the cooling under trees is reported to reduce heat stress directly: temperature under tree crowns in tropical pastures is 2 to 9°C lower than in open areas, with tree groups giving the largest reduction (3.6°C) and live fences the smallest (1.7°C) [ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2]. In Brazil's Caatinga, the black-globe temperature-humidity index fell from 89.2 to 84.2 and radiant thermal load also fell comparing shade under tree strips with sun exposure, and strips with the most woody cover were more efficient at mitigating cattle heat load than an almost treeless system, with the cooling effect holding even when the trees were leafless in the dry season [ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_3, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_2]. In Brazilian silvopasture compared with monoculture pasture, the area reaching critical thermal-comfort levels for animals fell by 20 to 100% [ev_microclimate_buffering_santos25_10]. A Peru/Colombia systematic review reports silvopastoral systems reduce paddock air temperature by up to 13°C on the hottest days [ev_microclimate_buffering_saucedo23_1]. The IPCC AR6 AFOLU chapter states in the same terms that agroforestry reduces ambient temperatures and crop heat stress [ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6_1]. More recent evidence adds further confirmation across livestock and crop systems. A review of cattle shade attributes trees as the most effective shade for livestock, combining sunlight protection with evaporative cooling from the leaves [ev_microclimate_buffering_blackshaw94_1]. Tree shading is reported to lower ambient temperatures by 4°C and soil temperatures by 6 to 10°C in tropical agroforestry, and shade trees are said to reduce canopy temperature by 2 to 4°C more generally, moderating severe temperature effects on understorey crops in wheat, coffee and silvopastoral systems [ev_microclimate_buffering_watts22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_patil25_4, ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_1]. In Costa Rica, measured shade reduced maximum air temperature by 1.7°C, with full-sun coffee leaves reaching up to 5°C above ambient air [ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_4]. CATIE reviews report tropical silvopasture 2 to 5°C cooler under tree crowns than outside them, and about 2°C cooler under tall (20 m) canopy specifically [ev_microclimate_buffering_montagnini15_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_montagnini15_2]. effect_mechanism: In rainfed cropping, trees and shelterbelts cool the crop. Under Faidherbia albida parkland trees in Ethiopia, midday air temperature at wheat floral height was lowered by up to 6°C against the open field, peaking at 29oC under the canopy versus 36oC outside [ev_microclimate_buffering_sida18_1]. A meta-analysis of Chinese farmland found shelterbelts reduced summer air temperature by 4.01% against unsheltered fields [ev_microclimate_buffering_hao26_1], and a review reports, second-hand, that poplar alley cropping in Germany was 3.4°C cooler than sole wheat on hot summer days [ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_4]. In semi-arid Kenya, dispersed Grevillea robusta trees over maize lowered the maize's own seasonal mean maximum growing-point temperature by 2.5 to 6.0 degrees C compared with unshaded sole maize, depending on the season [ev_microclimate_buffering_lott09_5].
conditionality: The row carries a harm signal: an FAO review in Senegal states, second-hand, that windbreak hedges generally cause a slight rise in temperature in the protected plots, with impacts varying by crop and growth stage, so shelter designs that cut wind may warm rather than cool [ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_16]. The units measure air temperature, a component of heat-stress impact, not heat-stress yield losses [ev_microclimate_buffering_sida18_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_hao26_1]. They span low-income Ethiopia, lower-middle-income Senegal, upper-middle-income China and high-income Germany [ev_microclimate_buffering_sida18_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_16, ev_microclimate_buffering_hao26_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_4]. effect_mechanism: Under tree crowns, temperature reductions of 2 to 9 °C relative to open areas have been reported, and in Cañas, Costa Rica, temperatures in the hottest hours were 3.6 °C, 2.9 °C and 1.7 °C lower under tree groups, single trees and live fences respectively than in open pasture [ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2]. Silvopastoral systems can reduce paddock air temperature by up to 13 °C on the hottest days, and trees in paddocks shade animals against excessive solar radiation, reducing heat stress [ev_microclimate_buffering_saucedo23_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_cisneros24_1]. In the dry Colombian Caribbean, silvopastoral models most intensive in shrubs, trees and rotational pasture reduce heat stress in cattle [ev_microclimate_buffering_murg13_1]. In Cuba live fences came to be used to shade cattle and avoid stress, and Neotropical livestock keepers value shade because it reduces heat stress and supports reproduction, weight gain and milk production [ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_3, ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_8]. In the semi-arid Caatinga of Brazil, the black globe temperature-humidity index fell from 89.2 in the sun to 84.2 in the shade of native tree strips at 10 am and 2 pm, the strips kept radiant thermal load and the index lower even when leafless in the dormant season, and a cited study found the silvopasture with more woody cover mitigated cattle heat load better [ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_2, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_3]. A systematic review of silvopastoral systems for dairy cows, mostly in Brazil, found the effect on the thermal environment was mostly (57%) favourable: silvopasture gave lower air temperature, black globe temperature, soil surface temperature, black globe humidity index and radiant thermal load than treeless pasture, and cows there showed fewer drinking events, lower surface temperature and lower respiratory rate [ev_microclimate_buffering_deniz23_1].
conditionality: Not every heat measure moved: in the same review, results for the temperature humidity index were unclear, with four of the seven studies that used it finding no significant difference from treeless pasture; the authors attribute this partly to that index leaving out solar radiation, the main pathway through which trees cut heat load [ev_microclimate_buffering_deniz23_2]. Most of the Latin American units are earlier studies cited in Spanish-language reviews, while the Brazilian Caatinga preprint and the dairy review rest on measurements [ev_microclimate_buffering_deniz23_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_2]; the Cuban and Neotropical shade units repeat Fudora et al. and Harvey et al., the latter a reading of livestock keepers' knowledge rather than a measurement [ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_3, ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_8]; the 13 °C figure is an upper value for the hottest days, and the Costa Rican units are high-income evidence [ev_microclimate_buffering_saucedo23_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2]. The units report air temperature, thermal indices or animal comfort, components of heat-stress impact rather than measured losses, and the evidence is mainly from upper-middle-income Latin America with a high-income Costa Rican unit [ev_microclimate_buffering_murg13_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_cisneros24_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2].

effect_mechanism: Shade trees in coffee and cocoa systems cool the canopy microclimate. A cocoa meta-analysis across ten countries found the canopy of shade trees keeps mean temperature lower and buffers daily maximum and minimum temperatures compared with monoculture, with potential to reduce the impact of rising mean temperatures and temperature extremes [ev_microclimate_buffering_niether20_1]. In Ghana, shade trees were confirmed to moderate the microclimate especially during dry and extremely dry periods, though daily mean maximum air temperatures still reached up to 44°C [ev_microclimate_buffering_abdul18_3]. In Costa Rica, shade reduces the maximum air temperature by 1.7°C and buffers air and soil temperature, reduces wind speed, and raises relative humidity and soil moisture under the canopy [ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_4, ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_9]. A review synthesis states shade trees reduce canopy temperatures by 2 to 4°C, mitigating heat stress [ev_microclimate_buffering_patil25_4], and in Central America shade trees are reported to have improved microclimate stability [ev_microclimate_buffering_patil25_7]. Across a multi-country tropical review, trees under canopies averaging 20 m tall gave a temperature reduction of about 2°C compared with a treeless site [ev_microclimate_buffering_montagnini15_2]. In Mexican coffee along a shade gradient, the high-shade site fluctuated least around the crop's optimum temperature of 20°C, staying closer to it than medium- and low-shade sites [ev_microclimate_buffering_lin07_1]. The IPCC AR6 WG2 chapter states shade trees can ameliorate increasing stand temperatures that would significantly affect arabica coffee [ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6ch5_2]. In Malaysian oil palm, alley-cropping with black pepper or cacao measured air temperature 1.3 °C and 1.2 °C cooler and soil-surface temperature 2.1 °C and 2.0 °C cooler than a 15-year-old monoculture, attributed to the alley crops' greater leaf area and ground cover intercepting radiation and reducing vertical mixing of warm air; against both the seven- and 15-year monocultures, the pepper and cacao alleys still measured significantly cooler soil-surface temperatures [ev_microclimate_buffering_ashraf19_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_ashraf19_3]. In Brazilian coffee, shaded plots measured consistently lower soil temperature at 10 cm depth than unshaded plots, and air temperature under shade had less day-to-day variation and a lower maximum than in the unshaded area [ev_microclimate_buffering_decarvalho21_3, ev_microclimate_buffering_decarvalho21_4].
conditionality: The same IPCC chapter immediately adds that the opposite can also be true, pointing to the drought-season soil-water competition recorded in the Ghanaian cocoa study above [ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6ch5_2, ev_microclimate_buffering_abdul18_3]. The same Patil review that found shade stabilising microclimate in Central America also reports that excessive shading combined with heavy rain raised the risk of fungal infection in parts of East Africa [ev_microclimate_buffering_patil25_7]. For seasonal mean temperature rather than day-to-day fluctuation, the Mexican coffee sites were not significantly different along the shade gradient, which the author reads as shade changing fluctuations more than seasonal means [ev_microclimate_buffering_lin07_2]. None of the ten units states a size for the gain beyond temperature differences of 1.7 to 4°C; none measures a severe or extreme heat event, only ordinary hot days or dry seasons [ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_4, ev_microclimate_buffering_patil25_4]. The evidence spans lower-middle, upper-middle, mostly-upper-middle and high-income cocoa and coffee countries across West and Central Africa, Southeast Asia and Latin America, so it transfers only as adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target [ev_microclimate_buffering_niether20_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_montagnini15_2, ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_4]. Against the cooling pattern, air temperature in the Malaysian pepper and cacao alleys did not differ from the age-matched seven-year-old monoculture, so the cooling shows up only against the older 15-year stand [ev_microclimate_buffering_ashraf19_2]; and bamboo and bactris alleys at the same site measured significantly hotter air (36.4 °C and 37.0 °C) than every other treatment, including both monocultures — a measured harm from the wrong alley crop, which the authors attribute to bamboo's sparse canopy, gaps and low ground cover leaving the soil exposed, concluding bamboo and bactris may not be appropriate intercrops for this reason [ev_microclimate_buffering_ashraf19_4]. Both sources are upper-middle-income evidence (Malaysia, Brazil), consistent with this row's existing transfer.

effect_mechanism: In the dry Colombian Caribbean, silvopastoral models most intensive in shrubs, trees and rotational pasture reduce heat stress in cattle, and a Brazilian study found agroforestry reduced the area at critical thermal-comfort levels for animals by 20 to 100% compared with monoculture pasture [ev_microclimate_buffering_murg13_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santos25_10]. In tropical silvopasture, temperatures under tree crowns can average 2-5°C lower than outside them throughout the year, depending on the characteristics of the trees [ev_microclimate_buffering_montagnini15_1]. Under tree crowns, temperature reductions of 2 to 9 °C relative to open areas have been reported, and in Cañas, Costa Rica, temperatures in the hottest hours were 3.6 °C, 2.9 °C and 1.7 °C lower under tree groups, single trees and live fences respectively than in open pasture [ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2]. Silvopastoral systems can reduce paddock air temperature by up to 13 °C on the hottest days, and trees in paddocks shade animals against excessive solar radiation, reducing heat stress [ev_microclimate_buffering_saucedo23_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_cisneros24_1]. In the semi-arid Caatinga of Brazil, the black globe temperature-humidity index fell from 89.2 in the sun to 84.2 in the shade of native tree strips at 10 am and 2 pm, the strips kept radiant thermal load and the index lower even when leafless in the dormant season, and a cited study found the silvopasture with more woody cover mitigated cattle heat load better [ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_2, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_3]. A systematic review of silvopasture and dairy cattle, mostly from Brazil, found the effect on the thermal environment was mostly (57%) favourable: silvopasture gave lower air temperature, black globe temperature, soil surface temperature and radiant thermal load than treeless pasture, and cows drank less often and had lower surface temperature and respiratory rate [ev_microclimate_buffering_deniz23_1]. An older review cites Kelly et al. (1950) that trees are the most effective shade for cattle, adding evaporative cooling from the leaves to protection from sunlight [ev_microclimate_buffering_blackshaw94_1].
conditionality: The Colombian and Brazilian review results are cited secondary findings from upper-middle-income settings, adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target [ev_microclimate_buffering_murg13_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santos25_10]. Most of the Latin American units are earlier studies cited in Spanish-language reviews, while the Brazilian Caatinga preprint measured the thermal indices itself [ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_2]; the 13 °C figure is an upper value for the hottest days, and the Costa Rican units are high-income evidence [ev_microclimate_buffering_saucedo23_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2]. All units report air temperature, thermal indices or animal comfort, components of heat-stress impact rather than measured losses [ev_microclimate_buffering_montagnini15_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_cisneros24_1]. Not every index moves: in the same systematic review, results for the temperature humidity index, which uses only air temperature and humidity, were unclear, with most of the studies that used it finding no significant difference between silvopasture and treeless pasture [ev_microclimate_buffering_deniz23_2]. The cattle-shade statement from Australia and the USA is an old citation without a tree system [ev_microclimate_buffering_blackshaw94_1].

effect_mechanism: The production evidence splits by sub-practice. Regeneration-based farmland, planted silvoarable systems and the cross-family syntheses each lean to a strong gain on their own, while silvopastoral, boundary and shaded perennial (coffee and cocoa) systems record both gains and losses. Meta-analyses report higher crop yield under agroforestry than controls in sub-Saharan Africa and higher soil nitrogen stocks than crop monocultures in the humid tropics, with soil nitrogen used here as a component of the production gap [ev_crop_yield_kuyah19_1, ev_soil_nitrogen_muchane20_1]. A meta-analysis cited in Arslan et al. (Branca et al.) associates agroforestry techniques with a 69% increase in cereal yields across the studies it consulted [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_14]. In the Sahel, millet yields are reported to double or triple under Faidherbia albida and yields were higher where intensive FMNR is practised, and tree shade in pastures is associated with gains in milk production and weight gain [ev_crop_yield_faosen24_8, ev_crop_yield_seghieri19_14, ev_livestock_productivity_murg13_4]. On paired on-farm plots in Ethiopia, wheat under Faidherbia albida crowns yielded 23-26% more grain than open-field wheat in the normal seasons of 2013 and 2014, and up to 85% more in 2015, an El Niño year in which both yields were low; available N close to the crowns was 35-55% larger than under sole wheat [ev_crop_yield_sida18_1, ev_crop_yield_sida18_2, ev_soil_nitrogen_sida18_1]. Lower yield variability under more diverse shade is cited as a sign of greater yield resistance to shocks in shaded systems, and Kenyan agroforestry-project farmers in Lower Nyando raised farm productivity against a control group [ev_crop_yield_morel24_4, ev_agricultural_production_value_thorlak12_1]. Fertilizer trees raise maize output: in Malawi, adopters had a 35% higher value of food crop production and 32% higher maize productivity than their counterfactual, and a review notes fertilizer tree species are widely documented to substantially increase maize yields compared with maize grown without fertilizer in Zambia and across Africa [ev_agricultural_production_value_coulibaly16_1, ev_crop_yield_coulibaly16_1, ev_crop_yield_lasco14_1]. In maize–Gliricidia trials run for 12-13 consecutive years in Malawi and Zambia, the intercrop gave the most stable yield at Makoka and more stable yields than fertilized maize at Msekera, and the intercrop with 50% of the recommended N and P fertilizer matched the yield of fully fertilized monoculture maize [ev_yield_stability_sileshi12_1, ev_yield_stability_sileshi12_2, ev_crop_yield_sileshi12_2]. Maize yields were more stable with Leucaena hedgerows than in monocrop, as also shown for alley cropping and fertilizer trees [ev_yield_stability_lasco14_1]. In Maradi, Niger, millet yields rose by 120 to 209 kg/ha where FMNR was older than 6 years, with smaller increases for younger FMNR, and FMNR is estimated to have raised yields by an average of 100 kg/ha over 5 million hectares [ev_crop_yield_abasse23_1, ev_crop_yield_abasse23_3]. In Lempira, Honduras, an ICRAF working paper reports that the Quesungual system raised maize yields from 1.9 to 3.2 tonnes per hectare and bean yields from 0.8 to 2.0 tonnes per hectare [ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_1, ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_2]. In Lempira, Honduras, farmers are reporting maize yield increases of a minimum of 60% after moving from slash-and-burn to the Quesungual system, and fields under continuous maize for seven years on 35% slopes and poor soil average 2.9 t/ha, against a best of 1.6 t/ha on the same fields before [ev_crop_yield_welc02_5, ev_crop_yield_welc02_6]. Under Sahelian parkland trees, tuber yield is improved (+0.40 to +1.67 t ha-1) and legumes are less affected than cereals, and tree fodder is crucial in the dry season and during drought [ev_crop_yield_bayala14_1, ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1]. A meta-analysis of Chinese farmland shelterbelts found crop yield 16.57% higher within sheltered farmland [ev_crop_yield_hao26_1]. In subarctic Ontario, a site lined by willow windbreaks produced about 300 g/m2 of bean pods against about 60 g/m2 at an open site, and potato tuber yield was 33% greater (3200 versus 2400 g/m2) [ev_crop_yield_barbeau18_1, ev_crop_yield_barbeau18_2]. In Colombian intensive silvopasture, milk production was 32.1% higher than with the same grasses without shrubs or trees, milk per hectare rose from 2 540 to 4 528 L a year with Leucaena, and silvopasture is cited as producing 12 times more beef than traditional grazing [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_3, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_1, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_3]. Intensive silvopasture raises stocking rates up to four times above extensive grazing and with them meat and milk output per hectare [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_1]. An IPCC climate-impacts assessment reports more generally that increased shade from trees or cost-effective structures can substantially reduce livestock heat stress and raise productivity [ev_livestock_productivity_porter14_1]. In Colombia, a Leucaena-based silvopastoral system raised stocking to 4.3 cows ha-1 while eliminating chemical fertiliser [ev_livestock_productivity_cisneros24_1]. In a mixed pasture of leucaena (Leucaena leucocephala) and the grass Setaria sphacelata, reported from Sri Lanka in the same review, nitrogen transferred from the tree gave the grass a 16% higher nitrogen yield than in monoculture, with 21% of the grass's nitrogen traced to the leucaena [ev_forage_productivity_dagang03_2]. In lowland Kenya, steers given incremental supplements of gliricidia (Gliricidia sepium) and leucaena forage alongside Napier grass gained 57% more live weight than steers fed Napier grass alone once the tree-legume forage reached 27% of total dry-matter intake [ev_livestock_productivity_dagang03_3]. A review also reports that integrating a grazed fodder bank — fodder trees or shrubs established on part of the pasture and then grazed — repeatedly raises animal production, though the gain is delayed by the trees' establishment period and by taking part of the pasture out of use while they establish [ev_livestock_productivity_dagang03_5]. In Colombia, forage production in a silvopastoral system of pastures, trees and Leucaena shrubs stayed constant in periods of intense drought while biomass in grass monoculture fell to 25%, and deep-rooted silvopasture trees are more drought-tolerant and give more stable forage volumes in the dry season [ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1, ev_forage_productivity_saucedo23_1]. Cattle in intensive silvopasture are better fed in critical drought periods, which reduces seasonal reproduction crises [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_2]. During El Niño events, milk production fell by 2.2% in silvopastoral systems against 4.9% in conventional systems [ev_livestock_productivity_guaqueta25_1]. At El Hatico, Colombia, the switch to intensive silvopasture allowed pasture irrigation to be dropped, and in 2009, the year with the lowest rainfall in several decades (440 mm), milk production still rose 10% on the previous year [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4]. Milk production rose 29% for cows on pasture with high tree density compared with low tree cover and above 15% in silvopasture compared with full sun, and dry-season weight gains were 2 to 5% higher on high tree-density pasture [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_1, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_3]. In shaded coffee and cocoa, a coffee meta-analysis found agroforestry reduced the odds of climate-related yield loss (OR = 0.69) and a cocoa meta-analysis found total system yields about ten times higher than in monocultures [ev_crop_yield_patil25_1, ev_crop_yield_niether20_2]. Planted legume trees in maize systems hold up in synthesis: a meta-analysis of studies from West, East and southern Africa put the maize yield response ratio at 1.27–1.43 after rotational improved fallows of non-coppicing woody legumes and 1.11–1.30 with relay intercrops, against unfertilised maize, and the yield increase was 1.6 t ha−1 with coppicing woody legumes [ev_crop_yield_sileshi08_1, ev_crop_yield_sileshi08_2, ev_crop_yield_sileshi08_3]. In the forest zone of Cameroon, maize grain yield in Leucaena alley plots rose from the first to the third year while yield in the treeless control fell, and groundnut in the alleys also out-yielded the control [ev_crop_yield_tonye95_1, ev_crop_yield_tonye95_2]. At Sadore, Niger, Ziziphus mauritiana trees raised sole millet yields by 41 % in the unfertilised control and by 10 % with farmyard manure, raised crop income by 5 to 14 % without counting the fruit, and from 2 to 3 times once fruit sales were included [ev_crop_yield_bado21_1, ev_crop_yield_bado21_2, ev_agricultural_production_value_bado21_1, ev_agricultural_production_value_bado21_2]. In Rwanda, Tephrosia vogelii intercropped in smallholder coffee and returned as mulch raised coffee yields by 400 kg ha−1, a 23–36% increase over the farmer's mulch practice across the two seasons [ev_crop_yield_bucagu13_1]. Among sub-Saharan adoption studies, high-quality maize studies show a significant gain for adopters (Cohen's d = 0.27, 95% CI: 0.12 to 0.42) [ev_crop_yield_jemaneh26_2]; a pest-control meta-analysis notes that the studies testing whether agroforestry pest control translated into crop yield both found it did [ev_crop_yield_pumarino15_1]; and a hedgerow meta-analysis found plant hedgerows raised soil total N (SMD = 1.33; 95% CI 0.98–1.68) [ev_soil_nitrogen_zheng20_1]. More recent additions to this evidence pool mostly repeat the same pattern. In Kenya, improved-fallow soil-fertility trials raised maize yield by a mean of 128% against no-input plots (median 167%), close to the 114% mean for biomass transfer and above the 89% mean for mineral fertiliser [ev_crop_yield_place05_1]. A pan-tropical meta-analysis found soil available nitrogen 46% higher under agroforestry than crop monocultures, with a mean response ratio of 1.46 [ev_soil_nitrogen_muchane20_2]. In Brazil, cassava under tree cover yielded up to 101.99 kg/ha against zero for the unshaded monoculture control in one season [ev_crop_yield_robusti17_1], and a review of coconut-based systems in Sri Lanka reports increased nut yields when pasture grasses, black pepper and coffee are intercropped with coconut [ev_crop_yield_kumar22_1]. More recent evidence adds further detail on shelterbelt and windbreak systems. In northeast China, shelterbelt-protected maize gained 4.28 to 9.45% at the optimal level of tree protection across climatic-productivity zones, largest in the semi-arid west [ev_crop_yield_zheng16_1, ev_crop_yield_zheng16_2, ev_crop_yield_zheng16_3]. A review of the worldwide windbreak literature finds field and forage crop yield generally higher in sheltered fields, with whole-field weighted mean gains of 20.8% in regions with persistent winter snow and 12.5% without it, and a net field-level spring wheat gain of 3.5% in Canada/USA once the competition zone, occupied land and sheltered zone are combined [ev_crop_yield_kort88_1, ev_crop_yield_kort88_6, ev_crop_yield_kort88_7, ev_crop_yield_kort88_5]. The Costa Rican livestock units are high-income evidence [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_3]. The cited 69% cereal-yield figure reaches this row second-hand through Arslan et al.: the citing text does not describe the agroforestry techniques further and reports no significance [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_14]. The newer evidence repeats these splits. Across sub-Saharan adoption studies agroforestry is not associated with a statistically significant effect on yield overall (Cohen's d = 0.35, 95% CI: −0.07 to 0.78, p = 0.14), the gain appearing only in the high-quality maize subset, and the review notes many adoption studies have weak causal identification [ev_crop_yield_jemaneh26_1, ev_crop_yield_jemaneh26_2]. In the Rwandan coffee trial the Tephrosia gain was significant only in the first season [ev_crop_yield_bucagu13_2], and a review of dairy silvopasture found no significant difference in milk production in the studies that measured it [ev_livestock_productivity_deniz23_1]. The Cambodian living-fence trial has no significance test reported for either the fodder yield or the cattle weight-gain comparison, the leucaena was grown on-station rather than harvested from an actual fence line (the living-fence framing is the authors'), and there was no comparator arm for the fodder yield beyond the dry-season feed gap with no tree fodder at all [ev_forage_productivity_gill20_1, ev_livestock_productivity_gill20_1]. The Ghanaian cocoa gain is modelled and confounded by uneven fertiliser use and hand pollination across the shade clusters it compares; the US and New Zealand forage results are measured but come from single, high-income temperate silvopasture trials, adding further support to the row's existing conflicting-evidence reading rather than resolving it [ev_crop_yield_hawkins24_2, ev_forage_productivity_orefice16_1, ev_forage_productivity_pollock08_1]. The Kenyan Grevillea seasons are four years of the same single trial site, not four independent sources, and the near-total yield losses occurred under a pruned, single-stem tree canopy [ev_crop_yield_lott09_1, ev_crop_yield_lott09_2, ev_crop_yield_lott09_3, ev_crop_yield_lott09_4]. The Brazilian alley-cropping figures are a single trial too, and its higher total-productivity and stability figures only hold once the trees' own fuelwood and fodder biomass are counted alongside the food crop, not for the food crop alone [ev_crop_yield_martins13_1, ev_crop_yield_martins13_2, ev_agricultural_production_value_martins13_1, ev_yield_stability_martins13_1]. The Indian biodrainage yield figures are a single planting in one location, and the wheat-yield gain is attributed to relief from waterlogging rather than any general agroforestry mechanism [ev_crop_yield_ram11_2, ev_crop_yield_ram11_3]. The Ghanaian, Ivorian and Brazilian shade-cocoa findings are all second-hand citations collected in a review editorial, not independently verified by this register, and the Brazilian one is confounded with a simultaneous fertiliser change [ev_crop_yield_vaast14_1, ev_crop_yield_vaast14_2, ev_crop_yield_vaast14_3].
