effect_mechanism: In high-income settings, agroforestry has been found both to raise and to lower output. Gains: in subarctic Ontario, a site lined by willow windbreaks produced about 300 g/m2 of bean pods against about 60 g/m2 at an open site, and potato tuber yield was 33% greater (3200 versus 2400 g/m2) [ev_crop_yield_barbeau18_1, ev_crop_yield_barbeau18_2]; cited studies from Cañas, Costa Rica found milk production more than 15% higher for cows grazing silvopasture than in full sun and dry-season weight gains 2 to 5% higher on high tree-density pasture [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_3]; and a cited Costa Rican study found moderate shade gave coffee yields similar to, or 3% higher than, full sun [ev_crop_yield_villa20_4]. Losses: a cited Costa Rican experiment recorded a 30% coffee yield reduction in the shaded system against coffee monoculture [ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_11]. On Saskatchewan prairie fields lined with old field shelterbelts, cereal yields next to the belt were depressed out to about 10 m from the field edge in all 3 years, a competition effect; the sheltered zone beyond it gave above-average yields in 1989 and 1990, but in 1991, a season with well above average water availability, that beneficial zone was absent [ev_crop_yield_kowa95_1, ev_crop_yield_kowa95_2, ev_crop_yield_kowa95_3]. Taking the mid-field yield as the reference, the authors estimate a net field yield loss equal to the width of the shelterbelt, though they doubt that mid-field is the right baseline [ev_crop_yield_kowa95_4]. A review of the worldwide windbreak literature adds a further measured contrast in Canada/USA spring wheat: yield in the competition zone right next to the belt (0.5 to 1 tree heights) fell 50% relative to unsheltered yield, yield in the sheltered zone further out (1 to 15 tree heights) was higher than unsheltered, and the net field-level yield across the whole 15-tree-height span, combining occupied land, the competition zone and the sheltered zone, was still 3.5% higher than unsheltered [ev_crop_yield_kort88_3, ev_crop_yield_kort88_4, ev_crop_yield_kort88_5].
conditionality: What separates the sides is the system and the competition for resources. The gains are livestock under tree cover and windbreak-sheltered vegetables in Ontario, where the plots were irrigated from ditches, whereas the losses are crops competing with trees: cereal next to Saskatchewan shelterbelts and established shade over coffee [ev_crop_yield_barbeau18_2, ev_crop_yield_kowa95_1, ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_11]. Distance from the trees and the season separate them within the shelterbelt study: yields were depressed next to the belt every year, higher in the sheltered zone in 1989 and 1990, and showed no sheltered gain in the wet 1991 season [ev_crop_yield_kowa95_1, ev_crop_yield_kowa95_2, ev_crop_yield_kowa95_3]. effect_mechanism: In upper-middle-income contexts, several studies show agroforestry or silvopasture raising production. In China, a national meta-analysis found crop yield 16.57% higher within sheltered farmland than unsheltered [ev_crop_yield_hao26_1], and a separate study of shelterbelt-protected maize in northeast China found yield gains of 4.28 to 9.45% at the optimal level of tree protection across climatic-productivity zones, highest in the semi-arid west [ev_crop_yield_zheng16_1, ev_crop_yield_zheng16_2, ev_crop_yield_zheng16_3]. In Iran, intercropped wheat and barley yielded 35% and 39% higher near trees than in their respective monocultures [ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_2]. In Brazil, second-year coffee yield under the best-performing shade-tree species reached up to 101.99 kg/ha while the unshaded monoculture control yielded nothing in the same year [ev_crop_yield_robusti17_1]. For livestock, Colombian intensive silvopasture raised milk production 32.1% over the same pasture grasses without shrubs or trees, and milk production still rose 10% in the lowest-rainfall year in several decades after a switch to intensive silvopasture that also allowed irrigation to be dropped [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_3, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4]. Leucaena-based silvopasture in Colombia raised stocking rate and milk output while eliminating chemical fertiliser, and a review reports silvopasture beef output 12-fold higher per unit of land than traditional grazing [ev_livestock_productivity_cisneros24_1, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_3]. In mixed crop-livestock Brazil, cattle in silvopasture gained 512 g/animal/day against 452 g/day in monoculture, and tree leaves added about 40 kg/ha of nitrogen in a cactus-pear-and-buffel-grass system, with potential to cut fertiliser costs [ev_livestock_productivity_santos25_12, ev_soil_nitrogen_santos25_7]. In Argentina, forage production under trees exceeded treeless grassland or pasture at drought intensities at or below the authors' dry-year threshold [ev_forage_productivity_peri24_1], and in Colombia forage production held steady through intense drought while grass monoculture biomass fell to a quarter [ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1]. In a mixed pasture of leucaena (Leucaena leucocephala) and the grass Setaria sphacelata, reported from Sri Lanka in the same review, nitrogen transferred from the tree gave the grass a 16% higher nitrogen yield than in monoculture, with 21% of the grass's nitrogen traced to the leucaena [ev_forage_productivity_dagang03_2]. A review also reports that integrating a grazed fodder bank — fodder trees or shrubs established on part of the pasture and then grazed — repeatedly raises animal production, though the gain is delayed by the trees' establishment period and by taking part of the pasture out of use while they establish [ev_livestock_productivity_dagang03_5]. In Brazil's semi-arid Cariri Paraibano, alley cropping cut maize-plus-bean biomass by about 38% against crops grown without trees over the whole experiment, though counting the trees' own leaf, twig and fuelwood biomass, total productivity in the tree system was 260% higher than in the treeless system, with biomass productivity also varying far less year to year (a coefficient of variation of 18.2% against 89.5%) [ev_crop_yield_martins13_1, ev_agricultural_production_value_martins13_1, ev_yield_stability_martins13_1]. On a set of monitored Bahia cocoa farms, removing shade trees entirely alongside fertiliser use nearly doubled cocoa bean yield [ev_crop_yield_vaast14_3].

In China, juvenile plumcot rows cut intercropped soybean yield by 46.03% and alfalfa hay yield by 51.83% against sole cropping, partly because the intercrop had less cropped area and a lower seeding rate [ev_crop_yield_wang23_1, ev_crop_yield_wang23_2]. In China, apricot-wheat intercropping significantly reduced wheat grain yield and its components in both years measured [ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_3]. In Brazilian agroforestry, soybean yielded only 500 to 700 kg/ha against about 2700 to 3000 kg/ha in monoculture over two seasons [ev_crop_yield_santos25_5]. In Indonesia, agroforestry maize yield was significantly lower by the third harvest, though soybean yield in the same system was unaffected across all three harvests [ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_4]. In Brazilian dairy, a review of silvopastoral studies found no significant difference in milk production in the studies that measured it, and under high-density Acacia decurrens silvopasture in Colombia, milk per cow per day was lower than in the open field, though lower-density silvopasture there still out-performed the open field [ev_livestock_productivity_deniz23_1, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_2]. During El Niño events, silvopastoral systems in Colombia lost less milk production than conventional systems, but still recorded a loss, not a gain [ev_livestock_productivity_guaqueta25_1]. In Brazil, drought-induced cocoa yield loss showed no relationship with shade-tree ground cover (p = 0.64), and in Mexico coffee harvest loss was unrelated to vegetation management, with all farms losing 18 to 40% of the harvest regardless of shade complexity [ev_crop_yield_gateau18_2, ev_crop_yield_philpott08_6]. In Argentina, the forage benefit itself is conditional and sometimes reverses: it held in very humid areas in both normal and dry years, showed no difference between systems in semi-arid areas, and at the semi-arid Santiago del Estero site swung from a slight gain in normal years to an 89% loss in a dry year, with denser tree canopy associated with lower relative forage production across sites [ev_forage_productivity_peri24_3, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_4, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_5, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_2, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_7]. The Brazilian alley-cropping figures are a single trial, and its higher total-productivity and stability figures only hold once the trees' own fuelwood and fodder biomass are counted alongside the food crop, not for the food crop alone [ev_crop_yield_martins13_1, ev_agricultural_production_value_martins13_1, ev_yield_stability_martins13_1]. effect_mechanism: Across silvopastoral systems, tree cover consistently raises forage and livestock output relative to open pasture. In Senegal, herbaceous biomass under Acacia tortilis and Balanites aegyptiaca canopies reached 2 to 5 times that measured in treeless areas, and tree leaves, fruit and pods make up about 40% of cattle diet and 80% of small-ruminant diet in the dry-to-wet-season transition [ev_forage_productivity_faosen24_20, ev_forage_productivity_faosen24_21]. Reviews report tree shade in pastures associated with 13 to 28% increases in milk production and weight gain generally [ev_livestock_productivity_murg13_4], and in Nicaragua and Costa Rica, milk production was 29% and over 15% higher on high tree-density or silvopasture compared with low-cover or full-sun pasture, with dry-season liveweight gains 2 to 5% higher on high-tree-density pasture, attributed to lower heat stress and more available foliage and fruit [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_1, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_3]. In Colombia, intensive silvopasture raised milk production 32.1% over the same pasture grasses without shrubs or trees, raised milk per hectare per year under Leucaena against an open-field system, and a review reports beef output 12-fold higher per unit of land than traditional grazing, also higher than improved treeless pasture [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_3, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_1, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_3]. Intensive silvopasture is also reported to raise stocking rate several-fold over extensive grazing, with proportional gains in meat and milk output, and better cattle feeding in critical drought periods is said to reduce seasonal reproduction crises [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_1, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_2]. During a severe drought, Colombian silvopastoral forage production held steady while grass-monoculture biomass fell to a quarter, and deep-rooted silvopasture trees are described as more drought-tolerant, giving more stable dry-season forage volumes [ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1, ev_forage_productivity_saucedo23_1]. A review also reports that integrating a grazed fodder bank — fodder trees or shrubs established on part of the pasture and then grazed — repeatedly raises animal production, though the gain is delayed by the trees' establishment period and by taking part of the pasture out of use while they establish [ev_livestock_productivity_dagang03_5]. In arid India, trees and shrubs lopped for green leaf fodder supply sheep, goats and camels with browse in drought years, when grass is scarce [ev_forage_productivity_singhrao08_2].
conditionality: Gains are not universal. Under high-density Acacia decurrens silvopasture in Colombia, milk per cow per day was lower than in the open field, though a lower-density silvopasture at the same site still out-performed the open field, showing tree density itself can flip the sign [ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_2]. A review of Brazilian silvopastoral thermal-comfort and production studies found no significant difference in milk production in the studies that measured it [ev_livestock_productivity_deniz23_1]. During El Niño events, silvopastoral systems in Colombia still lost milk production, just less than conventional systems did [ev_livestock_productivity_guaqueta25_1]. The Argentine multi-site forage evidence is the clearest statement that the benefit is severity- and site-dependent: it held in humid areas in both normal and dry years, showed no difference in semi-arid areas, and reversed from a slight gain to an 89% loss in a dry year at one semi-arid site, with denser canopy generally associated with lower relative forage production across sites [ev_forage_productivity_peri24_3, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_4, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_5, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_2, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_7]. Most of the Latin American livestock units are earlier studies cited in Spanish-language reviews or a CATIE edited volume rather than new primary measurements, and the clearest primary magnitudes (Colombia, Nicaragua, Costa Rica) are upper-middle or high income, while the Senegalese fodder evidence is lower-middle income, which is why this row's evidence sits adjacent to, rather than squarely inside, the LIC/LMIC target. Against this, a review of a regional silvopastoral conservation project in Esparza, Costa Rica reports that unpruned multistrata live fences can reduce forage availability by shading out the grasses along pasture edges [ev_forage_productivity_garbach12_1]. effect_mechanism: A sub-Saharan meta-analysis reports crop yield under agroforestry about twice that of non-agroforestry controls in the humid zone, and a pantropical meta-analysis finds higher soil nitrogen stocks than in crop monocultures, used here as a component [ev_crop_yield_kuyah19_1, ev_soil_nitrogen_muchane20_1]. A meta-analysis cited in Arslan et al. (Branca et al.) associates agroforestry techniques with a 69% increase in cereal yields across the studies it consulted [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_14]. IPCC assessments attribute higher land-equivalent ratios and large food-production benefits to well-planned agroforestry, and a cited review reports agroforestry systems 36-100% more productive than monoculture [ev_crop_yield_ipccar6ch5_8, ev_crop_yield_ipccsrccl6_3, ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_12]. In Lower Nyando, Kenya, farmers in an agroforestry project improved farm productivity on average against a control group [ev_agricultural_production_value_thorlak12_1]. A systematic review and meta-analysis of agroforestry adoption by smallholders in sub-Saharan Africa found a significant yield gain for maize in the high-quality studies (Cohen's d = 0.27, 95% CI: 0.12 to 0.42), and a pan-tropical meta-analysis of pest control reports that the only studies testing whether agroforestry pest control translated into crop yield both found a gain [ev_crop_yield_jemaneh26_2, ev_crop_yield_pumarino15_1].
conditionality: A systematic review's pooled crop-yield effect has a confidence interval spanning zero, the sub-Saharan adoption meta-analysis found that agroforestry overall is not associated with a statistically significant effect on yield (Cohen's d = 0.35, 95% CI: −0.07 to 0.78) [ev_crop_yield_jemaneh26_1], an integrative review counts 15 of 21 studies favouring agroforestry and 5 favouring monoculture, and another review notes trade-offs between crop intensification and ecosystem services in most agroforestry [ev_crop_yield_castle21s_1, ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_1, ev_crop_yield_vannoordwijk21_7]. The strong class therefore holds for well-designed tree–crop systems and for the better-quality studies; pooled adoption effects across all study types are smaller and less certain [ev_crop_yield_jemaneh26_1, ev_crop_yield_jemaneh26_2]. The pest-control yield link rests on very few studies cited in the meta-analysis (Ogol, Spence and Keddie 1999; Sileshi et al. 2005) [ev_crop_yield_pumarino15_1]. The cited 69% cereal-yield figure reaches this row second-hand through Arslan et al.: the citing text does not describe the agroforestry techniques further and reports no significance [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_14]. The pooled magnitude combines a crop-yield and a soil-nitrogen response ratio [ev_crop_yield_kuyah19_1, ev_soil_nitrogen_muchane20_1]. The Lower Nyando productivity gain had large standard errors and was not significant [ev_agricultural_production_value_thorlak12_1]. Livestock yield under linear agroforestry (alleys and windbreaks pooled) in a global review did not differ from the control: a 0.3% reduction with an even split of gains and losses over 36 paddock years [ev_livestock_productivity_baker25h2_13].

effect_mechanism: Linear tree plantings have been found both to raise and to lower yields. Gains come from shelter: windbreaks are reported to raise wheat yields by 15 to 20% by protecting plants from winter desiccation, protected plots in the Senegal River valley showed a 23 per cent total yield increase in the off-season, crop yield was 16.57% higher within sheltered farmland in a Chinese shelterbelt meta-analysis, and live fences can improve soil fertility and crop yields provided tree roots are deeper than crop roots [ev_crop_yield_dobhal24_7, ev_crop_yield_faosen24_13, ev_crop_yield_hao26_1, ev_crop_yield_moran18_11]. In subarctic Ontario, a site lined by willow windbreaks produced about 300 g/m2 of bean pods against about 60 g/m2 at an open site, and potato tuber yield was 33% greater (3200 versus 2400 g/m2) [ev_crop_yield_barbeau18_1, ev_crop_yield_barbeau18_2]. A meta-analysis of plant hedgerows found they raised soil total N (SMD = 1.33; 95% CI 0.98–1.68), counted here as a component of the production gap; hedgerow litter and the capture of nutrient-laden sediment from runoff supply it [ev_soil_nitrogen_zheng20_1]. Losses come from competition and shade: crop yield in shelterbelt edge zones fell by an average of 20.47% [ev_crop_yield_hao26_2], cereal yields next to Saskatchewan shelterbelts were depressed out to about 10 m from the field edge in all 3 years of a field study [ev_crop_yield_kowa95_1], excess shade can reduce pasture productivity [ev_livestock_productivity_moran18_14], and in the West African Sahel live fences and fodder banks reduced yields in the first year [ev_crop_yield_lasco14_2]. Hedgerow intercropping in a sub-Saharan meta-analysis gave a response ratio of 0.9, an interval touching no effect [ev_crop_yield_kuyah19_5]. A global quantitative review of paddocks with windbreaks found yield reduced by 8.3% on average against paddocks with no windbreaks, excluding the land occupied by the trees, with more decreases (n = 171) than increases (n = 83): crop yield −9.2% and crop biomass −9.3%, while pasture showed a small average increase of +3.1% [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_1, ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_2, ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_3, ev_forage_productivity_baker25h2_4]. In the same Saskatchewan study the sheltered zone beyond the competition strip gave above-average yields in 1989 and 1990, but against the mid-field yield the authors estimate a net field yield loss equal to the width of the shelterbelt, while doubting that baseline [ev_crop_yield_kowa95_2, ev_crop_yield_kowa95_4]. The global review's distance-response curves nonetheless predict a total yield change of +8.04% across a paddock 20 tree heights wide [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_5]. A review of the worldwide windbreak literature adds a further field/forage-crop verdict favouring shelter generally, with whole-field weighted mean yield gains of 20.8% in regions with persistent winter snow and 12.5% without it [ev_crop_yield_kort88_1, ev_crop_yield_kort88_6, ev_crop_yield_kort88_7]; within that literature, Canada/USA spring wheat yield was higher in the sheltered zone (1 to 15 tree heights) and the net field-level yield across the whole span was 3.5% above unsheltered [ev_crop_yield_kort88_4, ev_crop_yield_kort88_5]. In northeast China, shelterbelt-protected maize gained 4.28 to 9.45% at the optimal level of tree protection across climatic-productivity zones, the gain largest in the semi-arid west [ev_crop_yield_zheng16_1, ev_crop_yield_zheng16_2, ev_crop_yield_zheng16_3]. A Cambodian on-station trial of leucaena living fences adds further support: unirrigated leucaena still produced 2.8 to 6.5 kg of fresh fodder biomass per week per 100 trees right through the dry-season feed-gap period, and cattle supplemented with this fodder gained weight on average (4.2%) over a 107-day trial while control-group cattle fed only rice straw and local grass lost weight on average (0.7%) [ev_forage_productivity_gill20_1, ev_livestock_productivity_gill20_1].
conditionality: The evidence itself names most of what separates gains from losses. Distance from the trees: the same Chinese meta-analysis reports the field-scale gain and the edge-zone loss, which are not to be netted [ev_crop_yield_hao26_1, ev_crop_yield_hao26_2], and in Senegal yields fell within 10 metres of the hedges in the rainy season while the protected plots as a whole gained [ev_crop_yield_faosen24_13]. Root depth: the live-fence benefit is conditional on tree roots lying deeper than crop roots [ev_crop_yield_moran18_11]. Season: in the Saskatchewan study the sheltered-zone gain appeared in 1989 and 1990 but was absent in 1991, a season with well above average water availability, which the authors attribute to high actual evapotranspiration by the crops [ev_crop_yield_kowa95_2, ev_crop_yield_kowa95_3]. Time: the Sahel live-fence penalty was in the first year and yields recovered in the second [ev_crop_yield_lasco14_2]. Shade level: the pasture loss is from excess shade [ev_livestock_productivity_moran18_14]. These point to actionable design choices: species with deep roots, spacing and shade control, and accepting a first-year dip. At Bambey windbreak hedges had a neutral effect on groundnut [ev_crop_yield_faosen24_14]. On evidence quality, the hedgerow estimate is close to no effect rather than a clear loss [ev_crop_yield_kuyah19_5]; most other units are cited secondary results, the wheat figure has no stated location, and the Saskatchewan shelterbelt units are measured but high-income temperate evidence from Canada, outside the LIC/LMIC target [ev_crop_yield_dobhal24_7, ev_crop_yield_moran18_11, ev_crop_yield_kowa95_1]. Paddock geometry: the same review gives a pooled paddock loss and a predicted gain across a paddock 20 tree heights wide, so the width of the sheltered paddock relative to tree height separates loss from gain in its own data, consistent with the distance effect above [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_1, ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_5]. Crop type: in that review crop yield and biomass fell while pasture rose slightly, although the difference between yield types was not significant [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_2, ev_forage_productivity_baker25h2_4]. The global review's main text gives no country or income-group breakdown, so its losses cannot be placed against the LIC/LMIC target, and its windbreak group also takes in hedgerows and native forest blocks [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_1]. The Ontario windbreak gain is high-income boreal evidence from a single windbreak-lined site against a single open site, with plots irrigated from ditches, so it does not test competition next to the trees [ev_crop_yield_barbeau18_1, ev_crop_yield_barbeau18_2]. The hedgerow soil-nitrogen pool mixes grass-only strips with woody hedgerows and measures soil concentration, not yield, so it shows a pathway to higher output rather than the output itself [ev_soil_nitrogen_zheng20_1]. Against this, the same windbreak review notes that land occupied by the trees and tree-crop competition can turn the shelter gain into a net loss in some studies [ev_crop_yield_kort88_2], and its own Canada/USA wheat data show a 50% loss in the competition zone right next to the belt (0.5 to 1 tree heights), matching the Saskatchewan edge-zone loss already in this row [ev_crop_yield_kort88_3]. In northeast China, maize yield fell once shelterbelt density rose above the optimum, showing the same diminishing-returns pattern as the paddock-geometry and distance effects already described [ev_crop_yield_zheng16_4]. None of the Chinese or Canada/USA figures names a country-level income group beyond upper-middle or high, so this additional evidence does not shift the row's existing LIC/LMIC transfer. The Cambodian living-fence trial has no significance test reported for either the fodder yield or the cattle weight-gain comparison, the leucaena was grown on-station rather than harvested from an actual fence line (the living-fence framing is the authors'), and there was no comparator arm for the fodder yield beyond the dry-season feed gap with no tree fodder at all [ev_forage_productivity_gill20_1, ev_livestock_productivity_gill20_1].

The global review's distance-response curves nonetheless predict a total yield change of +8.04% across a paddock 20 tree heights wide [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_5]. A review of the worldwide windbreak literature adds a further field/forage-crop verdict favouring shelter generally, with whole-field weighted mean yield gains of 20.8% in regions with persistent winter snow and 12.5% without it [ev_crop_yield_kort88_1, ev_crop_yield_kort88_6, ev_crop_yield_kort88_7]; within that literature, Canada/USA spring wheat yield was higher in the sheltered zone (1 to 15 tree heights) and the net field-level yield across the whole span was 3.5% above unsheltered [ev_crop_yield_kort88_4, ev_crop_yield_kort88_5]. Distance from the trees: the same Chinese meta-analysis reports the field-scale gain and the edge-zone loss, which are not to be netted [ev_crop_yield_hao26_1, ev_crop_yield_hao26_2], and in Senegal yields fell within 10 metres of the hedges in the rainy season while the protected plots as a whole gained [ev_crop_yield_faosen24_13]. Root depth: the live-fence benefit is conditional on tree roots lying deeper than crop roots [ev_crop_yield_moran18_11]. Season: in the Saskatchewan study the sheltered-zone gain appeared in 1989 and 1990 but was absent in 1991, a season with well above average water availability, which the authors attribute to high actual evapotranspiration by the crops [ev_crop_yield_kowa95_2, ev_crop_yield_kowa95_3]. Time: the Sahel live-fence penalty was in the first year and yields recovered in the second [ev_crop_yield_lasco14_2]. Shade level: the pasture loss is from excess shade [ev_livestock_productivity_moran18_14]. These point to actionable design choices: species with deep roots, spacing and shade control, and accepting a first-year dip. At Bambey windbreak hedges had a neutral effect on groundnut [ev_crop_yield_faosen24_14]. On evidence quality, the hedgerow estimate is close to no effect rather than a clear loss [ev_crop_yield_kuyah19_5]; most other units are cited secondary results, the wheat figure has no stated location, and the Saskatchewan shelterbelt units are measured but high-income temperate evidence from Canada, outside the LIC/LMIC target [ev_crop_yield_dobhal24_7, ev_crop_yield_moran18_11, ev_crop_yield_kowa95_1]. Paddock geometry: the same review gives a pooled paddock loss and a predicted gain across a paddock 20 tree heights wide, so the width of the sheltered paddock relative to tree height separates loss from gain in its own data, consistent with the distance effect above [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_1, ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_5]. Crop type: in that review crop yield and biomass fell while pasture rose slightly, although the difference between yield types was not significant [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_2, ev_forage_productivity_baker25h2_4]. The global review's main text gives no country or income-group breakdown, so its losses cannot be placed against the LIC/LMIC target, and its windbreak group also takes in hedgerows and native forest blocks [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_1]. The Ontario windbreak gain is high-income boreal evidence from a single windbreak-lined site against a single open site, with plots irrigated from ditches, so it does not test competition next to the trees [ev_crop_yield_barbeau18_1, ev_crop_yield_barbeau18_2]. Against this, the same windbreak review notes that land occupied by the trees and tree-crop competition can turn the shelter gain into a net loss in some studies [ev_crop_yield_kort88_2], and its own Canada/USA wheat data show a 50% loss in the competition zone right next to the belt (0.5 to 1 tree heights), matching the Saskatchewan edge-zone loss already in this row [ev_crop_yield_kort88_3]. effect_mechanism: Fertiliser-tree and planted-alley systems raise crop yield and revenue across many Sahelian and sub-Saharan African sites. At Sadore, Niger, Ziziphus mauritiana trees raised sole millet yield by 41% in the unfertilised control and by 10% with farmyard manure, and raised gross crop revenue 5 to 14% excluding fruit, 2 to 3-fold once fruit sales were included [ev_crop_yield_bado21_1, ev_crop_yield_bado21_2, ev_agricultural_production_value_bado21_1, ev_agricultural_production_value_bado21_2]. In Malawi, fertilizer-tree (Gliricidia-based) adopters had a 35% higher value of food-crop production and 32% higher maize productivity than their modelled counterfactual [ev_agricultural_production_value_coulibaly16_1, ev_crop_yield_coulibaly16_1]. In Kenya, improved fallow (planted fertiliser trees) raised mean maize yield 128% (median 167%) over a no-input control [ev_crop_yield_place05_1]. A meta-analysis across West, East and southern Africa put the maize-yield response ratio at 1.27-1.43 after rotational improved fallows of non-coppicing woody legumes and 1.11-1.3 with relay intercrops against unfertilised maize, with a 1.6 t/ha gain from coppicing species [ev_crop_yield_sileshi08_1, ev_crop_yield_sileshi08_2, ev_crop_yield_sileshi08_3]. A sub-Saharan meta-analysis separately found crop-yield response ratios of 2.1 for alley cropping, 1.3 for dispersed tree intercropping and 2.6 for planted/improved fallow against non-agroforestry controls [ev_crop_yield_kuyah19_3, ev_crop_yield_kuyah19_4, ev_crop_yield_kuyah19_6]. In Cameroon, alley-cropped maize and groundnut out-yielded treeless controls across the trial years without added fertiliser [ev_crop_yield_tonye95_1, ev_crop_yield_tonye95_2]. In maize-Gliricidia trials in Malawi and Zambia, the intercrop gave more stable yields than monoculture maize across long-term seasons, and an intercrop with half the recommended fertiliser matched fully fertilised monoculture maize [ev_yield_stability_sileshi12_1, ev_yield_stability_sileshi12_2, ev_crop_yield_sileshi12_2]. In India, wheat grain yield rose 6.8% from reduced heat load under Populus deltoides [ev_crop_yield_dobhal24_6]. In Ethiopia, land productivity improved rapidly on about a fifth to a third of sites visited where nitrogen-fixing Acacia decurrens was incorporated into the farming system [ev_crop_yield_ieg20_1, ev_crop_yield_ieg20_2]. A Nigerian economic model of alley cropping on a 7% slope near Ibadan projects that, because lower cumulative soil loss sustains yield over a 20-year horizon, 2 m-spaced Leucaena alley cropping maintains the highest relative maize yield of five compared land-management systems, ahead of 4 m alley cropping, no-till and two bush-fallow rotations [ev_crop_yield_ehui90_4]. In semi-arid Kenya, a multi-season dispersed Grevillea robusta trial measured maize grain yield collapsing to a small fraction of the unshaded yield in every season: 0.06 against 1.80 t/ha in one season, 0.82 against 2.17 t/ha in another, 0.08 against 1.79 t/ha in a third, and 0.02 against 1.53 t/ha in a fourth, the worst seasons coinciding with low rainfall [ev_crop_yield_lott09_1, ev_crop_yield_lott09_2, ev_crop_yield_lott09_3, ev_crop_yield_lott09_4]. In Brazil's semi-arid Cariri Paraibano, alley cropping cut maize-plus-bean biomass by about 38% against crops grown without trees over the whole experiment, though a low-rainfall year gave very low yields in both systems with no significant difference between them, and counting the trees' own leaf, twig and fuelwood biomass, total productivity in the tree system was 260% higher than in the treeless system, with biomass productivity varying far less year to year (a coefficient of variation of 18.2% against 89.5%) [ev_crop_yield_martins13_1, ev_crop_yield_martins13_2, ev_agricultural_production_value_martins13_1, ev_yield_stability_martins13_1]. In canal-irrigated Haryana, India, a Eucalyptus biodrainage planting lowered the water table and raised wheat grain yield 3.4 times over compared with adjacent waterlogged fields, though near the tree lines shading and root competition cut wheat yield by an estimated 11.7% [ev_crop_yield_ram11_2, ev_crop_yield_ram11_3].
conditionality: The benefit is conditional on fertiliser treatment in the same Niger trial: the Ziziphus gain reversed to a 13% millet loss and a 4 to 11% loss for the millet/cowpea intercrop once NPK fertiliser was applied, and cowpea alone lost 15% without fertiliser (probably from tree shade), though it gained 9% with NPK (nitrogen from Ziziphus residues); soil total nitrogen did not differ significantly with and without the trees [ev_crop_yield_bado21_3, ev_crop_yield_bado21_7, ev_crop_yield_bado21_4, ev_crop_yield_bado21_5, ev_soil_nitrogen_bado21_1]. At Msekera, Zambia, fertilized monoculture maize out-yielded the maize-Gliricidia intercrop, and two of three stability models there ranked unfertilized control maize as more stable than the intercrop [ev_crop_yield_sileshi12_1, ev_yield_stability_sileshi12_3]. In Malawi, a Tephrosia relay intercrop (leafy residues, no grain) gave the same maize grain yield as monoculture maize fertilised the same way, so no yield gain from the relay crop itself [ev_crop_yield_snapp10_1]. In Kenya, the long-rains production-function estimate for improved fallow was not statistically significant [ev_crop_yield_place05_6]. Young, widely-spaced trees compete hard with the crop: in China, juvenile plumcot rows cut intercropped soybean yield 46.03% and alfalfa hay 51.83% against sole cropping, partly from less cropped area and lower seeding rate [ev_crop_yield_wang23_1, ev_crop_yield_wang23_2]; a review of alley systems found a mean paddock-level yield reduction of 17.63% (SD 36%, though 69 of 333 responses were increases), a predicted loss of more than 25% at spacings under 2.5 tree heights between alleys, and a 13% gain only at the widest spacing (15 tree heights) tested [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_6, ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_7, ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_8]; and in Kenya, a multi-season trial measured maize under dispersed Grevillea robusta trees collapsing to a small fraction of the unshaded yield in every season, the worst coinciding with low rainfall [ev_crop_yield_lott09_1, ev_crop_yield_lott09_2, ev_crop_yield_lott09_3, ev_crop_yield_lott09_4]. In France, a walnut-alley trial recorded winter pea yield consistently lower than the full-sun control, by 25 to 77% under normal rainfall and 1 to 47% under an imposed spring drought [ev_crop_yield_blan22_1, ev_crop_yield_blan22_2]. In China and Indonesia, intercropping cut wheat and third-harvest maize yield respectively against monoculture [ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_3, ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_4]. In Brazil, agroforestry soybean yielded only 500-700 kg/ha against about 2700-3000 kg/ha in monoculture [ev_crop_yield_santos25_5]. In Mozambique, a PES tree-planting intervention showed a negative crop-value proxy, against a strongly positive one for Malawi's fertiliser-tree programme in the same review [ev_crop_yield_castle21s_2, ev_crop_yield_castle21s_3]. A cross-regional review found trees had a negative effect on crop yields in 33% of African, 48% of Asian and 33% of American studies, even though the majority (52%) of cases overall were net positive or neutral, and it is based mostly (53 of 58 agroforestry studies) on trees introduced to open fields rather than agroforestry retained under a forest canopy [ev_crop_yield_reed17_1, ev_crop_yield_reed17_2, ev_crop_yield_reed17_3]. Most of the gain evidence (Niger, Malawi, Kenya, Cameroon, Ethiopia, the sub-Saharan meta-analyses) sits inside the LIC/LMIC target; the French, Chinese and some Indonesian/Iranian units are upper-middle or high income, outside it [ev_crop_yield_bado21_1, ev_agricultural_production_value_coulibaly16_1, ev_crop_yield_place05_1, ev_crop_yield_blan22_1, ev_crop_yield_wang23_1]. The Nigerian alley-cropping yield ranking is modelled rather than measured, running a simplified erosion model through a yield-loss function, and the alley yields are expressed per unit of cropped land only, not discounted for the land the hedgerows themselves occupy [ev_crop_yield_ehui90_4]. The Kenyan Grevillea seasons are four years of the same single trial site, not four independent sources [ev_crop_yield_lott09_1, ev_crop_yield_lott09_2, ev_crop_yield_lott09_3, ev_crop_yield_lott09_4]. The Brazilian alley-cropping figures are a single trial too, and its higher total-productivity and stability figures only hold once the trees' own fuelwood and fodder biomass are counted alongside the food crop [ev_crop_yield_martins13_1, ev_crop_yield_martins13_2, ev_agricultural_production_value_martins13_1, ev_yield_stability_martins13_1]. The Indian biodrainage yield figures are a single planting in one location, and the wheat-yield gain is attributed to relief from waterlogging rather than any general agroforestry mechanism [ev_crop_yield_ram11_2, ev_crop_yield_ram11_3]. Kenya and India are lower-middle income and Brazil is upper-middle, so the Kenyan and Indian findings sit inside the LIC/LMIC target and the Brazilian ones adjacent to it.

effect_mechanism: Regeneration-based farmland (FMNR and parkland systems) raises crop production mainly through nutrient addition under tree canopies and direct yield gains at the plot level. In Ethiopia, wheat under Faidherbia albida crowns yielded 23-26% more grain than open-field wheat in normal seasons (2013-2014), and up to 85% more in El Niño 2015, a dry year when both yields were low; available mineral nitrogen close to the crowns was 35-55% larger than under sole wheat [ev_crop_yield_sida18_1, ev_crop_yield_sida18_2, ev_soil_nitrogen_sida18_1]. In Senegal, millet yields are reported to double or even triple under F. albida canopy, and a meta-analysis reports mean yield increases of 150% for maize and 73% for sorghum under its canopy, alongside a significant 50% rise in total soil nitrogen, 21% in phosphorus and 32% in potassium [ev_crop_yield_faosen24_8, ev_crop_yield_faosen24_9, ev_soil_nitrogen_faosen24_2]. At Nioro-du-Rip, Senegal, millet grain yield with Piliostigma reticulatum was 886 kg/ha against 499 kg/ha without, at zero NPK [ev_crop_yield_seghieri19_15], and yields (millet and groundnut, plus fruit and wood) are higher on plots where intensive FMNR is practised [ev_crop_yield_seghieri19_14]. In Niger, soil nitrogen concentration was 38% higher under scattered shrubs than in open fields [ev_soil_nitrogen_felix18_1], and a pan-Sahelian review of 26 parkland references found millet and sorghum yields often higher in the presence of shrubs, ranging -25 to +120% [ev_crop_yield_felix18_1]; in Maradi, Niger, millet yields rose 120 to 209 kg/ha where FMNR was older than six years, and FMNR is estimated to have raised yields by an average of 100 kg/ha across 5 million hectares [ev_crop_yield_abasse23_1, ev_crop_yield_abasse23_3]. In Honduras, the Quesungual slash-and-mulch system raised maize yields from 1.9 to 3.2 t/ha and bean yields from 0.8 to 2.0 t/ha against the prior slash-and-burn system [ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_1, ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_2], and farmers report maize yield increases of a minimum of 60%, with the longest-running Quesungual fields averaging 2.9 t/ha against a best previous yield of 1.6 t/ha on the same steep, poor-soil fields [ev_crop_yield_welc02_5, ev_crop_yield_welc02_6]. In Ghana, 60% of FMNR-practising households reported increased farm yield from the same plot of land [ev_crop_yield_talensi21_1]. In the Sahel, moving from low to young-level FMNR significantly raised crop production [ev_crop_yield_bina15_5]. For livestock, herbaceous biomass under tree canopy in Senegal's Ferlo was 2 to 5 times that in treeless areas, and tree leaves, fruit and pods make up about 40% of cattle diet and 80% of small-ruminant diet in the dry-to-wet-season transition [ev_forage_productivity_faosen24_20, ev_forage_productivity_faosen24_21].
conditionality: Against this, the same Senegalese source reports measured harm: groundnut and millet yields fell under Cordyla pinnata canopy compared with outside the cover [ev_crop_yield_faosen24_11], and under parkland trees generally, cereal grain yield ranged from a loss under Balanites aegyptiaca to only a small gain under Faidherbia albida, attributed to competition for light, nutrients and water, while legumes were less affected and tubers improved [ev_crop_yield_bayala14_1]. Groundnut under F. albida itself behaves inconsistently across studies — one found a significant pod-yield rise, another variable yields, a third yield decreases [ev_crop_yield_faosen24_10]. In Niger, FMNR did not significantly raise cereal grain yields, with the authors attributing any income gain instead to crop diversification into higher-value crops [ev_crop_yield_haglund11_1], and moving from low to continuous FMNR gave no significant production gain in the Sahel, which the authors attribute to tree density and species quality [ev_crop_yield_bina15_6]. The pan-Sahelian parkland review that found yield gains under shrubs also found more variability under trees specifically, ranging from complete crop failure (-100%) to a tripling (+200%) [ev_crop_yield_felix18_2]. The Ethiopian temperature-cooling pathway only translated to a yield response once nitrogen was applied; without it, simulated wheat yield did not respond to the cooling at all, and total soil nitrogen itself showed no significant difference under versus outside the canopy at the end of one season despite the larger available nitrogen measured close to the crowns [ev_crop_yield_sida18_3, ev_crop_yield_sida18_4, ev_soil_nitrogen_sida18_2]. The Honduran and Ghanaian figures are farmer reports or project self-evaluations relayed by project-promoter staff or grey literature, not independently verified, and the Honduran comparator is the single best prior yield on the same fields, not an average [ev_crop_yield_welc02_5, ev_crop_yield_welc02_6, ev_crop_yield_talensi21_1]. All units sit in low and lower-middle-income West African and Central American drylands, in context with the LIC/LMIC target [ev_crop_yield_sida18_1, ev_crop_yield_felix18_1, ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_1].

effect_mechanism: In shaded coffee and cocoa systems, moderate shade levels can match or slightly exceed full-sun yield while raising the whole system's output. In Costa Rica, moderate shade gave coffee yields similar to or 3% higher than full-sun coffee, and no significant yield difference was found between lightly shaded (<30% cover) and full-sun coffee, with management intensity driving yield instead [ev_crop_yield_villa20_4, ev_crop_yield_villa20_3]. In Rwanda, a Tephrosia vogelii intercrop recycled as mulch in coffee raised parchment yield 23 to 36% over the farmer's own mulch practice across two seasons, though the gain was significant only in the first season [ev_crop_yield_bucagu13_1, ev_crop_yield_bucagu13_2]. A cocoa meta-analysis across ten countries found total system yield (cocoa plus all by-crops) about ten times higher in agroforestry than monoculture, even though cocoa-bean yield alone was lower [ev_crop_yield_niether20_2]. In Bolivia, total cocoa-system production was three times higher in agroforestry than monoculture [ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_9]. A coffee meta-analysis found agroforestry reduced the odds of climate-related yield loss relative to conventional coffee (odds ratio 0.69) and a moderate standardised mean difference favouring agroforestry across yield, bean size and quality outcomes [ev_crop_yield_patil25_1, ev_crop_yield_patil25_2]. Shade trees are also reported to reduce the biennial (boom-bust) oscillation of coffee yields, and lower yield variability under more diverse shade is read as greater resistance to shocks [ev_yield_stability_montagnini15_1, ev_crop_yield_morel24_4]. In Brazil, second-year coffee yield under the best-performing shade-tree species reached up to 101.99 kg/ha while the unshaded monoculture control yielded nothing [ev_crop_yield_robusti17_1]. Nitrogen-fixing shade trees (Erythrina poeppigiana, Inga edulis) fix around 100 kg N/ha in coffee systems, ranging 56 to 555 kg/ha across studies [ev_soil_nitrogen_villa20_12]. In Ethiopia, leguminous shade trees at high canopy openness strongly raised coffee yield in El Niño climate-shock years, and leguminous shade with low canopy openness also raised yield across all years [ev_crop_yield_morel24_1, ev_crop_yield_morel24_3]. In Ghana, whole-farm dry cocoa bean yield was positively associated with upper-canopy shade-tree cover in a model controlling for district, farm size and prior management [ev_crop_yield_asare18_1]. In Ghana, cocoa yield was 13% higher under moderate-shade hybrid cocoa than under full-sun hybrid cocoa [ev_crop_yield_hawkins24_2]. A cocoa-agroforestry review cites further shade-yield trade-offs: Ghanaian cocoa under moderate and heavy shade yielded 78% and 50% of the full-sun yield, Ivorian cocoa under mixed native shade had a far smaller pod harvest than full sun, and removing shade entirely alongside fertiliser use nearly doubled yield on a set of Brazilian farms [ev_crop_yield_vaast14_1, ev_crop_yield_vaast14_2, ev_crop_yield_vaast14_3].

The same ten-country cocoa meta-analysis that found a ten-fold total-system gain also found cocoa-bean yield alone 25% lower in agroforestry than full-sun monoculture [ev_crop_yield_niether20_1], a coffee/cocoa review found dry-bean yield per hectare 26% lower under shade than conventional [ev_crop_yield_jezeer17_1], in Bolivia a long-term randomised trial found cacao-bean yield 41% higher in full-sun monoculture than in agroforestry, though banana and plantain sales overcompensated for the agroforestry system's lower cacao revenue [ev_crop_yield_armengot16_1, ev_agricultural_production_value_armengot16_1], in Costa Rica coffee yield was 30% lower in agroforestry than monoculture once shade trees established [ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_11]. In a separate Nicaraguan sample, coffee productivity fell as shade-tree diversity rose, a relationship the authors call weakly significant once the lower investment on more diverse farms is accounted for, while productivity showed no significant residual relationship with shade-tree carbon stock [ev_crop_yield_hagg17_1, ev_crop_yield_hagg17_2]. In Cameroon, cocoa yields above 1.5 t/ha were only possible below 100-150 t C/ha of carbon storage, a direct yield-carbon trade-off [ev_crop_yield_seghieri19_6]. Several units found no significant yield effect either way: fruiting-node counts in 4-year-old shaded versus full-sun Costa Rican coffee, the shade-by-drought interaction on Ghanaian cocoa yield (shade did not prevent the drought-induced decline), drought yield loss against shade cover across Brazilian cocoa farms, coffee harvest loss against vegetation management in Mexico (all farms lost 18 to 40% regardless of shade complexity), coconut yield with interplanted trees in Kerala except where trees directly shade the palms, and galangal rhizome yield with or without over-canopy [ev_crop_yield_villa20_2, ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2, ev_crop_yield_gateau18_2, ev_crop_yield_philpott08_6, ev_crop_yield_kumar22_2, ev_crop_yield_kumar22_3]. Tree-cacao water competition under drought is separately reported to reduce soil moisture and push cacao yields below open-sun levels [ev_crop_yield_watts22_8]. A meta-regression found shade density, region, species and year did not significantly explain the variance in effect size across the pooled coffee studies, meaning the pooled average masks considerable site-to-site variation [ev_crop_yield_patil25_9]; soil nitrogen in the cocoa meta-analysis also did not differ significantly between agroforestry and monoculture, so the production gains there do not trace to measured soil fertility [ev_soil_nitrogen_niether20_1]. The clearest numeric losses (coffee, cocoa) come from Costa Rica, Bolivia, Ghana and a ten-country pool spanning lower-middle to high income; this cell is crop-specific to coffee and cocoa because shaded perennial-crop systems are judged on their host crop. This modelled estimate is confounded by uneven fertiliser use and hand pollination across the shade-density clusters the authors surveyed, and under optimal management the best full-sun clusters reached yields similar to the shaded ones, so the shade share of the gain is uncertain; it adds to the gain side of this row's existing split rather than resolving it [ev_crop_yield_hawkins24_2]. The Bolivian finding is now from the original trial rather than a second-hand reading, but it remains a single long-term trial [ev_crop_yield_armengot16_1, ev_agricultural_production_value_armengot16_1]. The Ghanaian, Ivorian and Brazilian shade-cocoa findings are all second-hand citations collected in a review editorial, not independently verified by this register, and the Brazilian one is confounded with a simultaneous fertiliser change [ev_crop_yield_vaast14_1, ev_crop_yield_vaast14_2, ev_crop_yield_vaast14_3].

effect_mechanism: Across silvopastoral systems, tree cover is widely reported to raise forage and livestock output relative to open pasture. In Colombia, intensive silvopasture raised milk production 32.1% over the same pasture grasses without shrubs or trees, and milk production still rose 10% in the lowest-rainfall year in several decades after converting to intensive silvopasture [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_3, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4]. A Leucaena-based silvopastoral system there raised stocking rate and milk output while eliminating chemical fertiliser, and milk per hectare per year rose over an open-field system, with beef output reported 12-fold higher per unit of land than traditional grazing [ev_livestock_productivity_cisneros24_1, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_1, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_3]. In Nicaragua and Costa Rica, milk production was 29% and over 15% higher on high tree-density or silvopasture than low-cover or full-sun pasture, with dry-season liveweight gains 2 to 5% higher on high-tree-density pasture, attributed to lower heat stress and more available forage [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_1, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_3]. Reviews report tree shade in pastures associated generally with 13 to 28% increases in milk production and weight gain, and intensive silvopasture raising stocking rate several-fold over extensive grazing with proportional gains in meat and milk output [ev_livestock_productivity_murg13_4, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_1]. In mixed crop-livestock Brazil, cattle in silvopasture gained 512 g/animal/day against 452 g/day in monoculture, and tree leaves added about 40 kg/ha of nitrogen in a cactus-pear-and-buffel-grass association [ev_livestock_productivity_santos25_12, ev_soil_nitrogen_santos25_7]. Through a severe drought, Colombian silvopastoral forage production held steady while grass-monoculture biomass fell to a quarter, and deep-rooted silvopasture trees are described as more drought-tolerant with more stable dry-season forage volumes [ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1, ev_forage_productivity_saucedo23_1]. In a mixed pasture of leucaena (Leucaena leucocephala) and the grass Setaria sphacelata, reported from Sri Lanka in the same review, nitrogen transferred from the tree gave the grass a 16% higher nitrogen yield than in monoculture, with 21% of the grass's nitrogen traced to the leucaena [ev_forage_productivity_dagang03_2]. In lowland Kenya, steers given incremental supplements of gliricidia (Gliricidia sepium) and leucaena forage alongside Napier grass gained 57% more live weight than steers fed Napier grass alone once the tree-legume forage reached 27% of total dry-matter intake [ev_livestock_productivity_dagang03_3]. A review also reports that integrating a grazed fodder bank — fodder trees or shrubs established on part of the pasture and then grazed — repeatedly raises animal production, though the gain is delayed by the trees' establishment period and by taking part of the pasture out of use while they establish [ev_livestock_productivity_dagang03_5]. An IPCC climate-impacts assessment reports more generally that increased shade from trees or cost-effective structures can substantially reduce livestock heat stress and raise productivity [ev_livestock_productivity_porter14_1]. In arid India, the same kind of trade-off shows up directly: a silvopasture trial measured lower understorey herbage yield under every tree and shrub species than in a treeless control during drought years, though the trees supplied extra dry-season browse fodder not counted in that herbage comparison [ev_forage_productivity_singhrao08_1, ev_forage_productivity_singhrao08_2].
conditionality: A global review of dispersed-tree (paddock-tree) silvopastoral systems against treeless controls found an average pasture-yield reduction of 20.8% (SD 41.2% across paddock-years) and a livestock-yield reduction of 18.6% on average (though 33% of paddock-years showed an increase); the loss worsens with tree density, reaching a predicted 30% reduction above 800 trees/ha and over 50% under the oldest dispersed trees reported, and livestock yield likewise declines with increasing tree density, then levels off, and declines further as the trees age [ev_forage_productivity_baker25h2_9, ev_livestock_productivity_baker25h2_14, ev_forage_productivity_baker25h2_10, ev_forage_productivity_baker25h2_12, ev_livestock_productivity_baker25h2_15, ev_livestock_productivity_baker25h2_16]. The same review found no effect of tree density on pasture yield under newly planted (young) dispersed trees, so the competition effect is one that builds up as trees establish and age, not a result of planting trees at all [ev_forage_productivity_baker25h2_11]. Density and age reverse the pattern elsewhere too: under high-density Acacia decurrens silvopasture in Colombia, milk per cow per day was lower than in the open field, though a lower-density silvopasture at the same site still out-performed the open field [ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_2]. A review of Brazilian silvopastoral studies found no significant difference in milk production in the studies that measured it [ev_livestock_productivity_deniz23_1], and during El Niño events, Colombian silvopastoral systems still lost milk production during the event, just less than conventional systems did [ev_livestock_productivity_guaqueta25_1]. The Argentine multi-site study is the clearest statement that the forage benefit is severity- and site-dependent: it held in humid areas in both normal and dry years, showed no difference in semi-arid areas, and reversed from a slight gain to an 89% loss in a dry year at one semi-arid site, with denser canopy generally associated with lower relative forage production across sites [ev_forage_productivity_peri24_3, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_4, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_5, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_2, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_7]. A further single-site silvopasture trial adds a directly measured establishment-phase loss: in New York, total forage dry matter was significantly lower under newly-established silvopasture than open pasture in the first year (255 against 409 kg/ha), which the authors attribute to volunteer grasses being slower to colonise under the retained trees; the gap was no longer significant by the second year, though the authors caution their small trial had little power to detect a real difference [ev_forage_productivity_orefice16_1, ev_forage_productivity_orefice16_2]. Tree age and dominance can also eliminate the forage altogether: in a New Zealand silvopasture, understorey pasture showed early complementarity with the young pines, but as the trees matured and came to dominate soil moisture, the pasture had disappeared entirely from under the trees by about 15 years into the rotation — the clearest statement in this row that the competition effect compounds with tree age, consistent with the global review's finding that density and age drive the loss [ev_forage_productivity_pollock08_1]. Both are single-site, high-income temperate trials (USA, New Zealand), adding to, rather than resolving, the row's existing gain/loss split. Against this, a review of a regional silvopastoral conservation project in Esparza, Costa Rica reports that unpruned multistrata live fences can reduce forage availability by shading out the grasses along pasture edges [ev_forage_productivity_garbach12_1].

effect_mechanism: Across sub-practices, agroforestry mostly raises household income and economic returns, with silvopastoral systems showing the strongest and most consistent gains. In Colombia, production costs were US$127/ha lower on average under intensive silvopastoral systems than traditional ranching, and the switch raised farmers' annual income by as much as US$523/ha [ev_household_income_cmscr20_6]; milk-sales income rose 42.12% under silvopasture, driven by higher stocking capacity (2.71 vs 1.84 animal units) [ev_household_income_montagnini15_1], and a benefit-cost ratio of 2.8 was found for an intensive silvopastoral system against 1.34 for a traditional system [ev_economic_return_saucedo23_1]. In shaded coffee and cocoa, a meta-analysis found net returns 23% higher on average in shaded systems, and a trend toward a higher benefit-cost ratio (1.66 against 1.44 for conventional systems) [ev_economic_return_jezeer17_1, ev_economic_return_jezeer17_2]. In India, a Gmelina-mango-pigeon pea agroforestry system gave net returns 1.67 to 2.72 times higher than the same species grown alone, with a benefit-cost ratio up to 2.33, and a biodrainage Eucalyptus strip planting in canal-irrigated Haryana, India earned farmers a benefit-cost ratio of 3.5:1 from selling the first rotation of trees, well above the 1.3:1 the same authors report for ordinary agricultural crops in Haryana [ev_economic_return_biswas22_1, ev_economic_return_ram11_4]. In Sudan, Acacia senegal intercropped with sorghum, sesame and roselle gave higher net revenue than any sole crop in a partial-budget analysis [ev_economic_return_fadl13_4, ev_economic_return_fadl13_5, ev_economic_return_fadl13_6]. In Kenya, improved-fallow agroforestry raised returns to labour to about US$2.17 a day, 33% higher than continuous maize with no inputs [ev_economic_return_place05_3]. In Nigeria, intercropping sweet orange with chilli pepper and amaranthus, or cassava and maize, gave a positive net present value against a negative NPV for monocropped orange [ev_economic_return_aiyel01_1]. Overall meta-analytic reviews find a positive but often small average effect: one puts the effect of agroforestry adoption on income at Cohen's d = 0.28 [ev_household_income_jemaneh26_1], and another at a standardised mean difference of 0.12, ranging up to 0.52 for a Kenyan climate-vulnerability-reduction programme [ev_household_income_castle21s_1, ev_household_income_castle21s_2]. In Nepal, the share of households below the poverty line fell from 48% in 2013 to 34% in 2016 after a market-oriented agroforestry intervention, with the steepest drop (62% to 28%) in one community [ev_rural_poverty_pandit19_1]. A Nigerian economic model of alley cropping near Ibadan compares the present value of incremental net returns (PVINR) of Leucaena alley cropping against a traditional bush-fallow control over a 20-year horizon. At the model's base-case discount rate, both 2 m and 4 m alley spacings show a positive incremental return against the control across the population-density scenarios tested, though in each scenario a long bush-fallow rotation still comes out ahead of alley cropping where land is abundant [ev_economic_return_ehui90_7, ev_economic_return_ehui90_8, ev_economic_return_ehui90_9, ev_economic_return_ehui90_10]. In Ghana, moderate-shade hybrid cocoa had by far the highest average plot profitability, with value of production 65% higher than under full-sun hybrid cocoa [ev_economic_return_hawkins24_3]. In a US forest-to-pasture conversion trial, silvopasture outperformed open pasture on both internal rate of return and net present value whether or not the initial timber-harvesting cost was included, because the retained trees add a long-term timber revenue while annual forage revenue, assumed equal in both systems, buffers the up-front harvest cost; silvopasture also gave a higher net present value than leaving the forest unmanaged for timber, and the highest net present value of all the options compared, including a thinned woodlot grown for wood alone [ev_economic_return_orefice16_1, ev_economic_return_orefice16_2, ev_economic_return_orefice16_3]. A CILSS regional synthesis adds two further Sahelian returns. For protecting natural regeneration on farmland in Niger, the internal rate of return was 31 percent, built from an initial investment of about 24 person-days of labour per hectare (1,000 FCFA per day, so 24,000 FCFA to start) against 20 years of wood production and a 5 percent millet and stalk gain in the first 4 years; fodder and soil-fertility benefits were left out of the calculation, so the authors consider the return an underestimate [ev_economic_return_botreij09_28]. On Burkina Faso's Central Plateau, farmer-managed natural regeneration returned an internal rate of 24 percent [ev_economic_return_botreij09_33]. In Bolivia, a long-term cacao trial found agroforestry's annual gross margin twice as high as full-sun monoculture, and its return per family working day almost twice as high too, mainly because banana and plantain sales made up for lower cacao revenue [ev_economic_return_armengot16_1, ev_economic_return_armengot16_2]. A Uganda restoration-opportunity assessment models a benefit-cost ratio of 13.6 for agroforestry at a 10% discount rate over a thirty-year horizon [ev_economic_return_mwe16_5].
conditionality: Against this, several units find losses or no effect. In Brazil, an agroforestry system's rice component showed negative economic performance needing adjustment, black pepper also turned unprofitable in low-price cycles, and a vegetable-heavy system collapsed from its seventh year through poor long-term management [ev_economic_return_ferraz24_6, ev_economic_return_ferraz24_5]. The same standardised-mean-difference review that found a 0.52 gain in Kenya found a −0.29 effect for crop-fruit tree intercropping in China [ev_household_income_castle21s_2], and in Nigeria, cut-and-carry mulching from multipurpose trees is profitable only where land and labour are abundant, turning unprofitable with negative returns where land is scarce [ev_economic_return_korm99_6]. In Nicaragua, net coffee revenue fell significantly as shade-tree diversity rose, a trade-off that held after accounting for lower investment on more diverse farms, though shade-tree carbon stock itself showed no significant relationship with either revenue or productivity [ev_economic_return_hagg17_1, ev_economic_return_hagg17_2]. In cocoa agroforestry across ten countries, total system production was higher than in monoculture but this was not reflected in higher revenues, net present values or lower costs [ev_economic_return_niether20_1]. In Ecuador, technified (less-shaded, more input-intensive) coffee management achieved the highest net margin per hectare against traditional, semi-intensive and organic (more-shaded) management — a signal that intensifying away from shade can out-earn the more agroforestry-like systems [ev_economic_return_perezneira16_1]. The Regreening Africa endline found more households selling tree products (rising from 8% to 20% overall, and sharply in Ghana and Mali), but average household income from tree products did not change overall, remaining at USD 82 (PPP) with wide variation by country [ev_household_income_rgaf23_6]. The World Bank's Colombian project found 47.2% of beneficiaries below the poverty line at baseline and could not yet attribute a clear poverty reduction, since many silvopastoral systems were still in their establishment phase and project effects were hard to separate from drought and other factors [ev_rural_poverty_cmscr20_9]. Most of the clearest gains (Colombia, Costa Rica, Sahel, Central America) sit inside the LIC/LMIC target, while the Ecuadorian, Chinese and Indonesian counter-signals sit in varied income contexts, so the row's strength is read from this balance rather than any single study [ev_economic_return_perezneira16_1, ev_household_income_castle21s_2, ev_economic_return_castle21s_4]. At a higher, sensitivity discount rate representing credit-constrained subsistence farmers, the same 2 m alley-cropping system reverses to a negative incremental return, less profitable than the more erosive bush-fallow control; the authors attribute this to alley cropping's establishment cost, since the Leucaena hedgerows take up to two years before giving any benefit — a measured harm the engine counts for some adopters alongside the other losses already in this row [ev_economic_return_ehui90_11]. All five figures are ordinal present-value rankings in Nigerian naira against the bush-fallow control, not comparable in absolute terms to the other currency figures already in this row, and all are modelled rather than measured, running a simplified erosion model through the same SCUAF framework used elsewhere in this register. The Ghanaian profitability gain is modelled, with wide and overlapping confidence intervals around the two shade groups, and the shade contrast is confounded by uneven fertiliser use and hand pollination; the US forest-to-pasture comparisons are a single-site model in a high-income temperate setting, outside the LIC/LMIC target, and the open-pasture comparator there carries the same timber-harvest cost, so none of this newer evidence shifts the row's existing moderate reading [ev_economic_return_hawkins24_3, ev_economic_return_orefice16_1]. Both are internal-rate-of-return figures from project tables with no significance test, read ordinally rather than compared in absolute terms with the currency figures elsewhere in this row [ev_economic_return_botreij09_28, ev_economic_return_botreij09_33]. Against this, modelling in Ghana finds certified shaded cocoa agroforestry less profitable than an assumed higher-yielding full-sun monoculture even with a certification premium, and a separate Ghanaian calculation of on-farm returns, including timber sales over 20 years, finds agroforestry not sufficiently attractive to farmers, with the certification premium not enough to offset the lost cocoa productivity [ev_economic_return_vaast14_4, ev_economic_return_vaast14_5]. Both Ghanaian findings are modelled, second-hand citations in a review editorial that assume the monoculture out-yields agroforestry by a fixed margin rather than measuring it. The Bolivian figures are a single long-term trial; the Uganda figure is an ex-ante appraisal built from assumed product and ecosystem-service values, not a measured outcome; and the Indian biodrainage ratio is a one-off harvest from a single planting [ev_economic_return_armengot16_1, ev_economic_return_armengot16_2, ev_economic_return_mwe16_5, ev_economic_return_ram11_4].

effect_mechanism: In irrigated cropland, trees bring returns from wood, fodder or fruit on top of the crop. A Senegalese review cites Fall et al. (2002) estimating that in the Senegal River valley a windbreak hedge in irrigated rice had an internal rate of return of 36 per cent, or 58 per cent when the woody products of the hedge were counted (Satin, 1998) [ev_economic_return_faosen24_15]. In canal-irrigated waterlogged fields at Hisar, India, a biodrainage study by Ram et al. found a benefit-cost ratio of 3.5:1 for the first rotation of Eucalyptus boundary strips, well above the 1.3:1 the same authors report for ordinary agricultural crops in Haryana, with returns from selling the trees after only an initial planting and maintenance cost [ev_economic_return_ram11_4]. In a drip-irrigated trial in Xinjiang, China, juvenile plumcot trees intercropped with alfalfa or soybean gave a higher average cash flow than the corresponding sole crops [ev_economic_return_wang23_1].
conditionality: How big the poverty effect is cannot be stated: the units report returns on investment or cash flow, components of household income rather than measured poverty change. The Senegalese figure is an earlier study read second-hand in a review [ev_economic_return_faosen24_15]. The Indian figure now comes from the original Ram et al. study rather than a second-hand reading, but it is still a single planting's first-rotation harvest, not a repeated or ongoing return [ev_economic_return_ram11_4]. effect_mechanism: An East African systematic review counts income among the main livelihood benefits of agroforestry, diversifying rural livelihoods and acting as a safety net in climate shocks, and calliandra fodder raised dairy farmers' net income in Kenya and Uganda [ev_household_income_muthuri23_1, ev_household_income_kiptot11_1]. Brazilian agroforestry viability studies report favourable financial indicators, and diversifying production and income is said to reduce farmers' vulnerability to commodity price volatility [ev_economic_return_ferraz24_1, ev_economic_return_ferraz24_7, ev_economic_return_ferraz24_8, ev_household_income_seghieri19_8]. A systematic review and meta-analysis of sub-Saharan adoption studies, mostly from Ethiopia, Kenya and Malawi, found agroforestry adoption raises household income (Cohen's d = 0.28, 95% CI: 0.13 to 0.44, p < 0.001), from diversified revenue in fruit, timber and fuelwood [ev_household_income_jemaneh26_1]. In the East Usambara Mountains, Tanzania, cash-crop revenues, especially from cardamom, and total income were significantly higher on farms using improved agroforestry, and gross income per capita was US$ 157 against US$ 74 on traditional farms [ev_household_income_reyes05_1]. In Rwanda, tree products are a safety net: food-insecure farmers more often sold tree products for income than food-secure farmers [ev_household_income_ndoli21_1]. In Nyando District, Kenya, agroforestry-project households sold fuel wood and timber to buy food during the drought, and in Lower Nyando held more livestock wealth than control households [ev_household_income_thorlak12_1, ev_household_income_thorlak12_2]. In a Mozambique carbon-forestry scheme promoting almost exclusively agroforestry, overall household income was generally increased [ev_household_income_lasco14_1]. In the Nepal mid-hills, after a market-oriented agroforestry project of fodder-tree hedgerows and understorey cash crops, bundled with marketing support, training, seed subsidies and organic fertiliser, the share of participating households below the poverty line dropped from 48 % to 34 % and the average farm-income figure rose from 37 to 48 percent, mainly from understorey crops, while off-farm income changed by -9% [ev_rural_poverty_pandit19_1, ev_household_income_pandit19_1]. In West Java, Indonesia, agroforestry had a higher net present value and benefit-cost ratio than swidden cultivation, according to a review's reading of Rahman et al. (2017) [ev_economic_return_ntawu23_2]. A Uganda restoration-opportunity assessment models a benefit-cost ratio of 13.6 for agroforestry at a 10% discount rate over a thirty-year horizon [ev_economic_return_mwe16_5].
conditionality: Several units show no effect or a loss: the pooled systematic-review income effect is not statistically significant, Regreening Africa found average tree-product income unchanged and no short-term income change detectable, and some Brazilian system components were loss-making [ev_household_income_castle21s_1, ev_household_income_rgaf23_6, ev_household_income_crs23_5, ev_economic_return_ferraz24_6]. The working paper's revenue measure is gross revenue, not profit, and not significant [ev_economic_return_steward23wp_1]. The Lower Nyando livestock-wealth difference, used by the authors as an income surrogate, was not significant at conventional levels, and the timber-sales finding is farmer-reported [ev_household_income_thorlak12_2, ev_household_income_thorlak12_1]. The Mozambique result is a review citation without an effect size [ev_household_income_lasco14_1]. The Nepal results come from a bundled project and are not credited in full to the trees: they are a before-and-after recall survey of participating households with no control group, and the share of the bundle due to agroforestry is not stated [ev_rural_poverty_pandit19_1, ev_household_income_pandit19_1]. The sub-Saharan pooled income effect rests on adopter versus non-adopter contrasts, many with weak causal identification, and its pool includes payments for ecosystem services in Mozambique, so part of that gain is a cash transfer rather than a production effect [ev_household_income_jemaneh26_1]. The Indonesian result is second-hand, from a small sample, and compares against swidden cultivation rather than permanent cropland [ev_economic_return_ntawu23_2]. effect_mechanism: In western Kenya, returns to labour from improved fallows were 33 percent higher than from no-input continuous maize, about 87.5% of Lower Nyando farmers who had their trees for 4 years reported income improvements, and a Mozambique PES tree-planting programme significantly raised cash income per capita [ev_economic_return_place05_3, ev_t6_income_timebenefit_castle21_6, ev_household_income_castle21s_6]. Fertilizer trees limit financial risk in drought years: where a crop fails, farmers using inorganic fertilizer lose the US$164 spent on the input, against US$90 for farmers who planted fertilizer trees [ev_economic_return_chaudhury11_1]. In southern Malawi, under higher fertiliser prices the value-cost ratio of a Tephrosia vogelii relay intercrop with maize stayed above 4.0, which the authors call a profitable scenario, while the higher prices pulled monoculture maize down to 2.5 or less [ev_economic_return_snapp10_1]. On-station and on-farm trials that cost both systems show trees with crops earning more than either alone: in Cameroon, Leucaena alley cropping without fertiliser gave a net benefit of US$4148 per hectare against US$2386 for the traditional treeless maize/groundnut intercrop [ev_economic_return_tonye95_1]; in North Kordofan, Sudan, crops grown in an Acacia senegal gum plantation out-earned the same crops grown alone: sorghum gave a net revenue of 558 SDG per hectare against 501 SDG as a sole crop, sesame 300 against 205, and roselle 518 against 389 [ev_economic_return_fadl13_4, ev_economic_return_fadl13_5, ev_economic_return_fadl13_6]; and in West Bengal, India, a Gmelina-mango-pigeon pea system gave net returns 2.66 times those of sole pigeon pea over a 10-year cycle, with a surge in the final year from the Gmelina timber harvest [ev_economic_return_biswas22_1]. effect_mechanism: FMNR and related regeneration-based farmland raise rural household income through tree products and diversified livelihoods. In the Sahel, moving from low to continuous Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) practice is associated with an increase in gross household income per capita of about 13%, through sale and own use of fuelwood, fodder, fruit, leaves and other products from the regenerated trees, and moving from low to new/young practice with a 10% increase in gross income through the same pathway [ev_household_income_bina15_2, ev_household_income_bina15_1]. In Niger, FMNR adoption raised gross annual household income by between 22,805 and 27,950 FCFA (46 to 56 USD) per capita, an 18 to 24% increase, with an estimated annual benefit-cost ratio of 2.5 to 3.0 and a 20-year net present value of €772/ha [ev_household_income_haglund11_1, ev_economic_return_haglund11_1, ev_economic_return_abasse23_1]. Sale of fuelwood and service wood from FMNR is reported to raise income across all social categories, including the very vulnerable [ev_household_income_abasse23_1]; a separate estimate put the annual value of FMNR, through improved soil fertility, firewood, fodder and other products, at US$56 per hectare in Niger [ev_economic_return_wvfmnr19_7], and the social return on investment of a Ghanaian FMNR project at US$655-887 per household per year [ev_economic_return_wvfmnr19_8]. In Senegal, FMNR-adopting households gained on average 72.65 USD per season from selling non-timber forest products, against 29.73 USD for non-adopters [ev_household_income_seghieri19_12]. In Honduras, farmers using the Quesungual slash-and-mulch system gained a new income stream from renting their land for livestock grazing, because the system produces more stover [ev_household_income_welc02_7]. Across its project countries, a World Vision meta-analysis found participants 15 percentage points more likely than non-participants to report an increase in household income and nine percentage points more likely to report a decrease in community poverty, an effect reported similarly by poorer households, female-headed households and female respondents [ev_household_income_wvfmnr19_5, ev_rural_poverty_wvfmnr19_10]. A WOCAT compiler for Kenyan FMNR rates farm income increased, noting diversified income from wood, honey, medicinal products and other non-wood products [ev_household_income_wocat_507_2019_farm_income]. A CILSS regional synthesis adds further Sahelian returns. For protecting natural regeneration on farmland in Niger, the internal rate of return was 31 percent, built from an initial investment of about 24 person-days of labour per hectare (1,000 FCFA per day, so 24,000 FCFA to start) against 20 years of wood production and a 5 percent millet and stalk gain in the first 4 years; fodder and soil-fertility benefits were left out of the calculation, so the authors consider the return an underestimate [ev_economic_return_botreij09_28]. On Burkina Faso's Central Plateau, farmer-managed natural regeneration returned an internal rate of 24 percent [ev_economic_return_botreij09_33].
conditionality: Against this, the same World Vision multi-country meta-analysis finds Uganda a clear outlier: participant households there were significantly less likely to report income improvements, which the authors attribute partly to participants being poorer households with different income-generation opportunities — the practice worsening the outcome for some adopters, counted here as measured harm [ev_household_income_wvfmnr19_6].
